subject: ems-sp
description: Economic & Management Sciences Senior Phase (Grades 7–9) question bank. One 20-item pool per atomic skill (the topic key IS the skill id). Content subject: 0.6 pass mark, mastery via lib/content-mastery.ts.

EMS.G7.E1.A1.title: Barter and early money
EMS.G7.E1.A1.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T1) — History of money: Barter and early money.
EMS.G7.E1.A1.recovery_strategy: Barter = swapping goods directly, with no money in between.

questions.question: What does it mean to trade by 'barter'?
options: Swapping one good directly for another
questions.expected: Swapping one good directly for another
questions.memo: Barter is exchanging goods or services directly for other goods or services, with no money in between.

questions.question: In a barter system, people exchange goods directly without using money.
questions.memo: Barter means swapping goods for goods — for example trading a bag of maize for a chicken — with no money involved.

questions.question: A farmer wants to swap maize for shoes, but the shoemaker does not want maize. What problem of barter is this?
options: Both people must want what the other has
Money is too heavy to carry
The farmer has no bank account
questions.expected: Both people must want what the other has
questions.memo: Barter only works when each person wants what the other is offering — this is the 'double coincidence of wants'.

questions.question: Trading goods directly for other goods, without money, is called ____.
questions.memo: Barter is the direct exchange of goods for goods — the oldest way of trading.

questions.question: Why did people start looking for something better than barter?
options: It was hard to find someone who wanted exactly what you had
questions.expected: It was hard to find someone who wanted exactly what you had
questions.memo: Barter is slow and difficult because you must find a person who both has what you want and wants what you have.

questions.question: A promissory note is a written promise to pay someone an amount of money.
questions.memo: A promissory note is an early form of paper money — a written promise to pay a stated amount.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of bartering?
options: Trading two goats for a sack of salt
Swiping a card at a shop
questions.expected: Trading two goats for a sack of salt
questions.memo: Bartering is swapping goods for goods — like goats for salt — without any money changing hands.

questions.question: In early societies, why were goods like cattle, salt or shells sometimes used as a form of money?
options: People generally accepted and valued them
They were printed by a bank
They could not be eaten or used
questions.expected: People generally accepted and valued them
questions.memo: Before coins, useful and widely-valued goods such as cattle or salt were accepted in exchange because most people wanted them.

questions.question: Barter works only when both people want what the other is offering — a problem called the double coincidence of ____.
questions.memo: The 'double coincidence of wants' means each trader must want exactly what the other has — the main weakness of barter.

questions.question: Bartering large or valuable items, like a cow, made it easy to buy something small and cheap.
questions.memo: You cannot split a cow to buy a loaf of bread — bartering large items for small ones is very awkward, another weakness of barter.

questions.question: Which is a disadvantage of a barter system?
options: Goods like food can spoil before you trade them
Goods can be swapped instantly anywhere
It needs no people at all
questions.expected: Goods like food can spoil before you trade them
questions.memo: Many barter goods (like food) do not store well, so wealth could rot away before it was traded — a real weakness of barter.

questions.question: Long ago, traditional societies most often got the things they needed by ____.
questions.memo: Before money existed, traditional societies traded by bartering goods and services directly.

questions.question: Money was invented partly to solve the problems of bartering.
questions.memo: Money made trade easier by removing barter's main problem — needing to find someone who wanted exactly what you had.

questions.question: Which situation would make barter easiest?
options: Two people each want exactly what the other has
Everyone wants the same single item
questions.expected: Two people each want exactly what the other has
questions.memo: Barter is simplest when there is a double coincidence of wants — each person wants what the other offers.

questions.question: A written promise to pay an amount of money is called a ____ note.
questions.memo: A promissory note records a promise to pay a set amount — an early step towards paper money.

questions.question: In a barter economy you always need a bank to make a trade.
questions.memo: Barter needs no bank and no money — just two people willing to swap goods directly.

questions.question: Which pair shows a barter exchange?
options: Fixing a fence in return for a bag of oranges
questions.expected: Fixing a fence in return for a bag of oranges
questions.memo: Swapping a service (fixing a fence) for goods (oranges), with no money, is barter.

questions.question: Put the development of trade in the order it happened in history.

items.text: People barter goods directly for other goods
Useful goods like salt or cattle are used as money
Written promises to pay (promissory notes) appear
Modern money is used for everyday trade

questions.memo: Trade moved from direct barter, to using valued goods as money, to written promises to pay, and finally to modern money.

questions.question: Sort each example into 'Barter' or 'Using money'.

items.text: Swapping a chicken for a bag of mealies
Tapping a card to buy airtime

questions.expected: Swapping chicken for mealies and firewood for fish are barter; paying cash or by card uses money.
questions.memo: Barter swaps goods for goods; using money means one side pays with cash or a card instead of goods.

questions.question: Which best explains why barter is slow and difficult?
options: You must find someone who wants your goods and has what you want
Goods are always free in barter
There is too much money around
questions.expected: You must find someone who wants your goods and has what you want
questions.memo: Barter needs a double match of wants, so finding the right trading partner is slow and often difficult.

EMS.G7.E1.A2.title: Coins and paper money
EMS.G7.E1.A2.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T1) — History of money: Coins and paper money.
EMS.G7.E1.A2.recovery_strategy: Money solved barter's problem: you no longer need a perfect match to trade.

questions.question: What were the first coins usually made from?
questions.memo: Early coins were made from metals such as gold, silver and copper, which were valued and lasted a long time.

questions.question: Paper money is lighter and easier to carry than a large amount of coins.
questions.memo: Paper money lets people carry a high value in a light, small form — much easier than heavy coins.

questions.question: Why was money like coins a better way to trade than barter?
options: It is widely accepted, so you don't need a double match of wants
It only works for one person
It cannot be divided into smaller amounts
questions.expected: It is widely accepted, so you don't need a double match of wants
questions.memo: Because almost everyone accepts money, you can sell to one person and buy from another — no need to find a double coincidence of wants.

questions.question: Money made from metal, stamped into a round shape with a set value, is called a ____.
questions.memo: A coin is a piece of metal with a set value, used as money.

questions.question: Which is an advantage of coins over bartering cattle?
options: Coins can be divided into small values for small purchases
questions.expected: Coins can be divided into small values for small purchases
questions.memo: Coins come in small denominations, so you can pay exact amounts — unlike a cow, which you cannot split.

questions.question: Paper money was introduced partly because carrying lots of heavy coins was inconvenient.
questions.memo: Large amounts of coins are heavy and awkward, so lighter paper money was introduced to make trade easier.

questions.question: Compared with food used as money, why is metal money more useful?
options: Metal does not spoil and lasts a long time
questions.expected: Metal does not spoil and lasts a long time
questions.memo: Money needs to store value over time; metal lasts and does not rot, unlike food.

questions.question: Money printed on paper, such as a R100 ____, is light and easy to carry.
questions.memo: Paper money comes as notes (like a R100 note), which are light and carry high value.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of paper money?
questions.memo: A banknote is paper money; a coin is metal money, and a card is not money itself but a way to access it.

questions.question: Once people accepted coins and notes, trade between strangers became easier.
questions.memo: Widely-accepted money means even strangers can trade, because both trust the money will be accepted again.

questions.question: Why do coins and notes have different values printed on them (like 50c, R10, R100)?
options: So people can pay different amounts exactly
To make them harder to use
So they can spoil at different speeds
questions.expected: So people can pay different amounts exactly
questions.memo: Different denominations let people make up almost any amount and pay exactly, which barter could never do.

questions.question: Coins and paper money only have value if people are willing to accept them.
questions.memo: Money works because people trust and accept it; without that acceptance, a note is just paper.

questions.question: Which is a disadvantage of carrying a large amount of coins?
options: They cannot be used to buy anything
questions.memo: A large value in coins is heavy and bulky to carry — one reason paper money became popular.

questions.question: Coins are usually made of ____, while notes are made of paper.
questions.memo: Coins are metal and notes are paper — two common forms of cash.

questions.question: Which statement about money is correct?
options: Money is widely accepted as payment for goods and services
Money can only be used once
Money must be swapped for the exact same item
questions.expected: Money is widely accepted as payment for goods and services
questions.memo: A key feature of money is that it is generally accepted as payment, which is what makes trade easy.

questions.question: A bank card is the same thing as paper money.
questions.memo: A bank card is not money itself — it is a tool that lets you spend the money held in your bank account.

questions.question: Both coins and paper money work as money mainly because they are ____.
options: generally accepted by everyone in trade
printed by each person at home
questions.expected: generally accepted by everyone in trade
questions.memo: Coins and notes work because people generally accept them as payment — that shared acceptance is what gives money its use.

questions.question: Put these forms of money in the order they generally appeared in history.
questions.memo: Money developed from valued goods, to metal coins, to paper notes, and most recently to electronic payments.

questions.question: Sort each item into 'Coin' or 'Paper money (note)'.
questions.expected: R5 and 50c are coins; the R100 and R50 are paper notes.
questions.memo: Coins are the metal pieces (50c, R5); notes are the printed paper money (R50, R100).

questions.question: What is the main reason money replaced barter in most societies?
options: Money makes trading faster and easier
questions.expected: Money makes trading faster and easier
questions.memo: Money is widely accepted and easy to divide and carry, so it makes trade much faster and easier than barter.

EMS.G7.E1.A3.title: Electronic banking and the role of money
EMS.G7.E1.A3.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T1) — History of money: Electronic banking and the role of money.
EMS.G7.E1.A3.recovery_strategy: Money does three jobs: it pays, it stores wealth, and it prices things.

questions.question: What is electronic banking?
options: Managing money and making payments using computers and phones
Storing coins in a jar at home
questions.expected: Managing money and making payments using computers and phones
questions.memo: Electronic banking lets people move money and pay for things digitally, using cards, apps and the internet.

questions.question: An EFT (electronic funds transfer) moves money from one bank account to another without cash.
questions.memo: An EFT shifts money electronically between accounts — no physical cash is handled.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of electronic banking?
questions.memo: Using a card to pay is electronic banking; the others are barter or cash.

questions.question: Using a phone app or card to pay, instead of cash, is part of ____ banking.
questions.memo: Electronic banking covers digital ways of paying and managing money, such as apps and cards.

questions.question: Money lets you buy goods and services today. This role of money is called a ____.
questions.memo: As a medium of exchange, money is the thing everyone accepts to buy and sell goods and services.

questions.question: When you keep money to use later, money is acting as a ____.
questions.memo: Money can be saved and used later, so it stores value over time — as long as prices stay fairly stable.

questions.question: A price tag of R20 lets you compare the value of different goods. This role of money is a ____.
questions.memo: Money acts as a measure (or unit) of value: prices let us compare how much different things are worth.

questions.question: One advantage of electronic banking is that you do not have to carry large amounts of cash.
questions.memo: Paying electronically is safer and more convenient because you avoid carrying lots of cash.

questions.question: Money that everyone accepts when buying and selling is acting as a medium of ____.
questions.memo: As a medium of exchange, money is accepted by all in trade, removing the need for barter.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the three main roles of money?
questions.memo: Money's three roles are medium of exchange, store of value and measure of value — spoiling food is not one of them.

questions.question: Saving money in a bank account is an example of money being used as a store of value.
questions.memo: Money kept in a bank holds its value for future use, which is the 'store of value' role.

questions.question: Why is a bank card useful for electronic banking?
options: It lets you spend money in your account without cash
It can be eaten if you are hungry
questions.expected: It lets you spend money in your account without cash
questions.memo: A card gives you access to the money in your account so you can pay digitally, without handling cash.

questions.question: Mandla checks his balance and pays a shop using his phone. This shows ____.
questions.memo: Checking a balance and paying by phone are everyday examples of electronic banking.

questions.question: Because a price in rands tells us what something is worth, money works as a ____ of value.
questions.memo: Prices let us measure and compare value, so money is a measure (unit) of value.

questions.question: With electronic banking, money can be sent to another person in another town in minutes.
questions.memo: Electronic transfers move money quickly between accounts, even over long distances.

questions.question: Which is a possible disadvantage of electronic banking?
options: You need a device and a network connection to use it
It can only be used once
questions.expected: You need a device and a network connection to use it
questions.memo: Electronic banking depends on having a phone or card and a working connection — a problem if these are not available.

questions.question: Which everyday action uses money as a medium of exchange?
options: Buying a loaf of bread with cash
Reading a price tag to compare two shirts
Writing your name on a form
questions.expected: Buying a loaf of bread with cash
questions.memo: Spending money to buy something now is money working as a medium of exchange.

questions.question: Match each use of money to the role it shows by ordering them: exchange, store, then measure.

items.text: Paying cash for a taxi ride (using money to buy now)
Keeping R500 in a bank for next year (holding value)
Reading price tags to compare two phones (comparing value)

questions.memo: Buying now = medium of exchange; saving for later = store of value; comparing prices = measure of value.

questions.question: Sort each payment into 'Cash' or 'Electronic banking'.

items.text: Sending an EFT on a banking app

questions.expected: Notes and coins are cash; card taps and EFTs are electronic banking.
questions.memo: Cash means physical notes and coins; electronic banking means digital payments like cards and EFTs.

questions.question: Money has only one role: to be saved.
questions.memo: Money has three roles — a medium of exchange, a store of value, and a measure of value — not just saving.

EMS.G7.E2.A1.title: Needs of individuals to countries
EMS.G7.E2.A1.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T1) — Needs and wants: Needs of individuals to countries.
EMS.G7.E2.A1.recovery_strategy: A need is something you must have to live; bigger groups have bigger needs.

questions.question: What is a 'need'?
options: Something you must have to live
Something nice to have but not essential
questions.expected: Something you must have to live
questions.memo: A need is something essential for survival, such as food, water, shelter and clothing.

questions.question: Food, water, shelter and clothing are basic needs of every person.
questions.memo: These are the basic needs everyone must meet to stay alive and healthy.

questions.question: Which is a need of a whole community rather than just one person?
options: A clinic and clean water supply
A child's single pair of shoes
questions.expected: A clinic and clean water supply
questions.memo: Communities have shared needs like clinics, water supply and roads that serve many people at once.

questions.question: Something a person must have in order to survive is called a ____.
questions.memo: A need is essential for survival; a want is something extra that is nice to have.

questions.question: Which of these is a need of a country (rather than a single family)?
options: Hospitals, roads and electricity for everyone
questions.expected: Hospitals, roads and electricity for everyone
questions.memo: A country must provide large-scale needs — hospitals, roads, electricity — for all its people.

questions.question: The needs of a country are usually bigger and more expensive than the needs of one family.
questions.memo: A country must meet the needs of millions of people, so its needs are far larger than a single family's.

questions.question: A family's need for shelter is usually met by ____.
questions.memo: Shelter is a basic need, met by a home; the others are wants, not needs.

questions.question: A school, a clinic and clean water are examples of the needs of a whole ____.
questions.memo: These are shared needs of a community, used by many people together.

questions.question: Why do individuals, families, communities and countries all have needs?
options: All of them must meet basic requirements to function and survive
questions.expected: All of them must meet basic requirements to function and survive
questions.memo: At every level — person, family, community, country — basic needs must be met for life to work.

questions.question: A want is something you must have to stay alive.
questions.memo: That describes a need. A want is something extra and nice to have, not essential for survival.

questions.question: Which list contains only basic needs?
questions.memo: Food, water and shelter are basic needs; the others are wants.

questions.question: As you move from an individual to a country, the needs generally become ____.
options: larger and shared by more people
questions.expected: larger and shared by more people
questions.memo: Bigger groups have bigger, shared needs — a country must serve millions, not one person.

questions.question: Clean water is a need shared by individuals, families, communities and countries.
questions.memo: Everyone needs clean water — it is a basic need at every level of society.

questions.question: Roads, electricity and hospitals are large needs that a whole ____ must provide.
questions.memo: A country provides large-scale needs like roads, electricity and hospitals for all its people.

questions.question: Which best shows the difference between a family need and a country need?
options: A family needs a home; a country needs housing for millions
A country needs less than a family
questions.expected: A family needs a home; a country needs housing for millions
questions.memo: A family meets its own shelter need; a country must plan housing for the whole population.

questions.question: Communities sometimes work together to meet shared needs like a clinic or a water tap.
questions.memo: Shared community needs are often met by people and government working together.

questions.question: Put these needs in order from the smallest group to the largest group they serve.

items.text: A family's groceries for the week

questions.memo: Needs grow from individual, to family, to community, to a whole country.

questions.question: Sort each need by who it mainly serves.

items.text: Electricity supply for the whole nation

questions.expected: Meals and shoes are individual/family needs; roads and national electricity are country needs.
questions.memo: Small, personal needs are met by individuals and families; large, shared needs are met at country level.

questions.question: Which statement is correct?
options: Needs exist at every level, from a single person to a whole country
Needs disappear as groups get bigger
questions.expected: Needs exist at every level, from a single person to a whole country
questions.memo: Individuals, families, communities and countries all have needs — they just differ in size.

questions.question: Individuals, families, communities and countries all have needs.
questions.memo: Needs exist at every level of society, growing larger as the group grows.

EMS.G7.E2.A2.title: Primary and secondary needs
EMS.G7.E2.A2.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T1) — Needs and wants: Primary and secondary needs.
EMS.G7.E2.A2.recovery_strategy: Primary = survival; secondary = comfort and quality of life.

questions.question: What is a primary need?
options: A basic need you must have to survive
A need that makes life more comfortable
questions.expected: A basic need you must have to survive
questions.memo: Primary needs are essential for survival — food, water, shelter, clothing.

questions.question: Secondary needs make life better and more comfortable but are not needed for basic survival.
questions.memo: Secondary needs (like education or transport) improve quality of life but are not survival essentials.

questions.question: Which is a primary need?
questions.memo: Water is essential for survival, so it is a primary need; the others are wants or secondary.

questions.question: Needs that are essential for survival, like food and shelter, are called ____ needs.
questions.memo: Primary needs are the basics required to stay alive.

questions.question: Which is best described as a secondary need?
questions.memo: Education improves life and prospects but is not needed for immediate survival, so it is a secondary need.

questions.question: Food is a secondary need.
questions.memo: Food is a primary need — you cannot survive without it.

questions.question: Why do we call food, water, shelter and clothing 'primary' needs?
options: They must be met first because life depends on them
They are only wanted by some people
questions.expected: They must be met first because life depends on them
questions.memo: Primary needs come first because survival depends on them.

questions.question: Needs that improve comfort and quality of life, like transport or education, are ____ needs.
questions.memo: Secondary needs raise the quality of life but are not survival essentials.

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches primary and secondary needs?
questions.memo: Food is a survival need (primary); a smartphone improves life but isn't essential (secondary).

questions.question: If primary needs are not met, a person's life and health are at risk.
questions.memo: Without food, water or shelter, survival itself is threatened — that is why they are primary.

questions.question: A family with very little money should usually meet which needs first?
options: Primary needs like food and shelter
questions.expected: Primary needs like food and shelter
questions.memo: Limited money should go to survival first — primary needs before secondary needs or wants.

questions.question: Which best describes the order in which needs should be satisfied?
options: Primary needs first, then secondary needs
questions.expected: Primary needs first, then secondary needs
questions.memo: Survival needs come first; comfort and improvement needs come after.

questions.question: Clothing to keep warm is a primary need.
questions.memo: Clothing for protection and warmth is essential for survival, so it is a primary need.

questions.question: Because you can survive without it, a holiday is an example of a ____ need or a want.
questions.memo: A holiday is not essential to survive, so it is at best a secondary need (often a want).

questions.question: Which of these would normally be ranked as the most urgent need?
questions.memo: Drinking water is a survival essential, making it the most urgent primary need on the list.

questions.question: Both primary and secondary needs are important, but primary needs come first.
questions.memo: Secondary needs matter for quality of life, yet survival needs must be met first.

questions.question: Put these needs in the order most people would satisfy them, from first to last.
questions.memo: Survival needs (food, water, shelter) come first, then quality-of-life needs like education, then wants like holidays.

questions.question: Sort each item into 'Primary need' or 'Secondary need'.
questions.expected: Food and shelter are primary; education and transport are secondary.
questions.memo: Primary = survival essentials; secondary = things that improve life but aren't needed to survive.

questions.question: Which statement is TRUE about primary and secondary needs?
options: Primary needs are essential; secondary needs improve quality of life
Secondary needs are essential; primary needs are extras
They mean exactly the same thing
questions.expected: Primary needs are essential; secondary needs improve quality of life
questions.memo: Primary needs are survival essentials; secondary needs make life more comfortable.

questions.question: Shelter and clothing are primary needs because they help us survive.
questions.memo: Shelter and warm clothing protect life and health, so they are primary needs.

EMS.G7.E2.A3.title: Unlimited wants, limited resources
EMS.G7.E2.A3.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T1) — Needs and wants: Unlimited wants, limited resources.
EMS.G7.E2.A3.recovery_strategy: We can't have everything — limited resources force us to choose.

questions.question: Why can't people satisfy all their wants?
options: Wants are unlimited but resources are limited
questions.expected: Wants are unlimited but resources are limited
questions.memo: People always want more, but the resources (money, time, materials) to meet those wants are limited.

questions.question: Human wants are unlimited.
questions.memo: People always desire more goods and services, so wants are described as unlimited.

questions.question: Because resources are limited, people and countries must make ____.
questions.memo: Limited resources force us to choose what to satisfy first and what to give up.

questions.question: When there is not enough of something to satisfy everyone's wants, we call this ____.
questions.memo: Scarcity means resources are limited compared with unlimited wants.

questions.question: A learner has R20 and wants both a burger (R20) and a movie (R20). What must they do?
options: Choose one because resources are limited
questions.expected: Choose one because resources are limited
questions.memo: With only R20, the learner must choose — a clear example of limited resources forcing a choice.

questions.question: If money and resources were truly unlimited, there would be no need to choose.
questions.memo: Choice is only necessary because resources are limited; unlimited resources would remove the need to choose.

questions.question: Which of these is a limited resource?
options: The number of wants people have
questions.memo: Money is a limited resource; wants and wishes, by contrast, are unlimited.

questions.question: Because we cannot have everything, choosing one thing means giving up ____.
questions.memo: Every choice has a trade-off: choosing one want usually means giving up another.

questions.question: What is the main reason economies have to make choices about what to produce?
questions.memo: Scarcity of resources forces economies to choose what, how and for whom to produce.

questions.question: A 'want' is something extra that we would like, even if we can live without it.
questions.memo: Wants are things we desire beyond our basic needs; we can survive without them.

questions.question: Which best describes the economic problem?
questions.memo: The basic economic problem is that wants are unlimited while resources to meet them are limited.

questions.question: When a family chooses to spend money on school fees instead of a TV, this shows ____.
options: making a choice because resources are limited
questions.expected: making a choice because resources are limited
questions.memo: Limited money means the family must choose between options — fees over a TV.

questions.question: Scarcity affects individuals, but it does not affect whole countries.
questions.memo: Scarcity affects everyone, including countries, which also have limited resources and must make choices.

questions.question: The thing you give up when you choose something else is the ____ of your choice.
questions.memo: Every choice has a cost — the next-best thing you gave up to get it.

questions.question: Which statement about wants and resources is correct?
options: People want more than the available resources can provide
questions.expected: People want more than the available resources can provide
questions.memo: Unlimited wants outstrip limited resources, which is why choices must be made.

questions.question: Making good choices helps people use their limited resources wisely.
questions.memo: Since resources are limited, wise choices help people get the most value from what they have.

questions.question: Put these decision steps in order for a learner with limited pocket money.

items.text: Choose it and give up the others for now

questions.memo: Limited resources → list wants → prioritise → choose and accept the trade-off.

questions.question: Sort each item into 'Unlimited' or 'Limited'.
questions.expected: Wants and wishes are unlimited; money and time are limited resources.
questions.memo: Wants keep growing (unlimited); resources like money and time run out (limited).

questions.question: The fact that wants are unlimited but resources are limited is known as the problem of ____.
questions.memo: Scarcity — limited resources against unlimited wants — is the central problem in economics.

questions.question: Because resources are limited, we cannot satisfy every want.
questions.memo: Limited resources mean some wants must always go unmet, forcing choices.

EMS.G7.E3.A1.title: Goods versus services
EMS.G7.E3.A1.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T1) — Goods and services: Goods versus services.
EMS.G7.E3.A1.recovery_strategy: A good is a thing you can touch; a service is a job done for you.

questions.question: What is a 'good'?
options: A physical thing you can touch and own
A job someone does for you
questions.expected: A physical thing you can touch and own
questions.memo: A good is a physical product, like bread or a phone, that you can touch and own.

questions.question: A service is work done for you by someone else, like a haircut or a taxi ride.
questions.memo: A service is an action or task performed for you; you cannot hold it like a physical good.

questions.question: Which of these is a service?
questions.memo: A doctor's examination is a service (work done for you); the others are physical goods.

questions.question: A physical product you can touch, like a school bag, is called a ____.
questions.memo: Goods are tangible products you can touch and own.

questions.question: Which of these is a good?
options: A bus driver taking you to school
questions.memo: A cellphone is a physical good; the others are services.

questions.question: You can store a good for later, but a service is usually used at the moment it is provided.
questions.memo: Goods can be kept; services are generally consumed as they happen (a haircut can't be stored).

questions.question: What is the main difference between a good and a service?
options: A good is a physical thing; a service is an action done for you
A good is free; a service costs money
A good is digital; a service is physical
questions.expected: A good is a physical thing; a service is an action done for you
questions.memo: Goods are tangible products; services are tasks or actions performed for someone.

questions.question: Cutting someone's hair is an example of a ____.
questions.memo: A haircut is work done for a customer, so it is a service.

questions.question: Which list contains only goods?
options: A haircut, a taxi ride, a lesson
A bus trip, bread, a phone
questions.memo: Bread, shoes and a phone are all physical goods; the other lists mix in services.

questions.question: Electricity supplied to your home is usually treated as a service.
questions.memo: Supplying electricity is a service you pay for; the supplier provides it continuously.

questions.question: A spaza shop sells cold drinks and also lets customers buy airtime. The cold drink is a ____ and selling airtime is a ____.
questions.memo: The cold drink is a physical good; providing airtime is a service.

questions.question: Which is the best example of a service in a community?
questions.memo: Collecting rubbish is a service performed for the community; the others are goods.

questions.question: A motor mechanic repairing a car is providing a good, not a service.
questions.memo: Repairing a car is work done for the owner, so it is a service, even though parts (goods) may be used.

questions.question: Goods and ____ are the two things produced in an economy to satisfy needs and wants.
questions.memo: Economies produce both goods (products) and services (tasks done for people).

questions.question: Why are both goods and services important in an economy?
options: Both are needed to satisfy people's needs and wants
questions.expected: Both are needed to satisfy people's needs and wants
questions.memo: People need both physical products and helpful services to meet their needs and wants.

questions.question: A bottle of cooldrink is a good because you can touch and keep it.
questions.memo: It is a physical, storable product, which makes it a good.

questions.question: Put these steps in order for getting a service at a hair salon.

items.text: You leave with a fresh haircut

questions.memo: A service is delivered as it happens — you receive the haircut at the moment it is done.

questions.question: Sort each item into 'Good' or 'Service'.
questions.expected: Bread and takkies are goods; a taxi ride and a nurse's care are services.
questions.memo: Goods are physical products; services are tasks or actions done for you.

questions.question: Which statement is correct?
options: Goods are products you can touch; services are useful actions done for you
Goods and services are the same thing
Goods are tasks done for people
questions.expected: Goods are products you can touch; services are useful actions done for you
questions.memo: Goods are tangible; services are intangible actions performed for someone.

questions.question: Unlike a good, a service usually cannot be touched or stored.
questions.memo: Services are actions done for you; they are used as they happen and cannot be stored like goods.

EMS.G7.E3.A2.title: Producers and consumers
EMS.G7.E3.A2.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T1) — Goods and services: Producers and consumers.
EMS.G7.E3.A2.recovery_strategy: Households earn by producing and spend by consuming.

questions.question: Who is a producer?
options: Someone who makes goods or provides services
questions.expected: Someone who makes goods or provides services
questions.memo: A producer makes goods or provides services for others to use.

questions.question: A consumer is a person who buys and uses goods and services.
questions.memo: A consumer is the person who buys and uses what producers make.

questions.question: Which is an example of a producer?
questions.memo: A baker produces the bread; the others are consumers or just observers.

questions.question: A person who buys and uses goods and services is called a ____.
questions.memo: Consumers buy and use the goods and services that producers supply.

questions.question: How can a household be a producer?
questions.memo: Household members produce by working — providing labour — for which they earn an income.

questions.question: A household can be both a producer and a consumer.
questions.memo: Households produce by working and earning, and consume by buying goods and services — so they are both.

questions.question: When a family buys groceries, the family is acting as a ____.
questions.memo: Buying and using goods makes the family a consumer.

questions.question: Someone who makes goods or provides services is a ____.
questions.memo: Producers create the goods and services that consumers use.

questions.question: Which best shows a household acting as a producer?
options: A parent going to work and earning a wage
questions.expected: A parent going to work and earning a wage
questions.memo: Working and earning is producing (supplying labour); the rest are consuming.

questions.question: Producers and consumers depend on each other.
questions.memo: Producers need consumers to buy their goods, and consumers need producers to supply them — they depend on each other.

questions.question: A farmer grows vegetables and sells them at a market. At the market the farmer is a ____, and the people buying are ____.
questions.memo: The farmer produces and sells; the buyers consume.

questions.question: Why do producers make goods and services?
options: To sell them to consumers and earn an income
To keep them all for themselves
questions.expected: To sell them to consumers and earn an income
questions.memo: Producers aim to sell to consumers and earn an income or profit.

questions.question: Only businesses can be producers; households never produce anything.
questions.memo: Households also produce — for example by supplying labour to businesses — so they are producers too.

questions.question: Producers and consumers ____ on each other in the economy.
questions.memo: The economy works because producers and consumers rely on one another.

questions.question: A learner who buys a cooldrink and also helps in the family shop after school is acting as ____.
options: both a consumer and a producer
questions.expected: both a consumer and a producer
questions.memo: Buying the cooldrink is consuming; helping in the shop is producing — so the learner is both.

questions.question: A consumer uses goods and services to satisfy needs and wants.
questions.memo: Consumers buy and use goods and services to meet their needs and wants.

questions.question: Put the flow between producer and consumer in the right order.

items.text: The good is offered for sale

questions.memo: Goods flow from producer, to sale, to the consumer who buys and uses them.

questions.question: Sort each role into 'Producer' or 'Consumer'.

items.text: A tailor sewing dresses to sell
A worker earning wages at a factory

questions.expected: The tailor and the factory worker are producers; the dress buyer and the family are consumers.
questions.memo: Producers make or supply; consumers buy and use.

questions.question: Which statement is correct?
options: Households can act as both producers and consumers
questions.expected: Households can act as both producers and consumers
questions.memo: Households consume (buy and use) and produce (supply labour), so they are both.

questions.question: A baker who bakes and sells bread is acting as a producer.
questions.memo: Making and selling goods makes the baker a producer.

EMS.G7.E3.A3.title: Using goods and services wisely
EMS.G7.E3.A3.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T1) — Goods and services: Using goods and services wisely.
EMS.G7.E3.A3.recovery_strategy: Efficient use and recycling make limited resources go further.

questions.question: What does it mean to use resources 'efficiently'?
options: Getting the most use out of them with little waste
questions.expected: Getting the most use out of them with little waste
questions.memo: Efficient use means making the most of resources while wasting as little as possible.

questions.question: Recycling helps us reuse materials and reduce waste.
questions.memo: Recycling turns used materials into new products, reducing waste and saving resources.

questions.question: Which is an example of reusing a good?
options: Refilling a glass bottle instead of throwing it away
Throwing a bottle in the bin
Buying a new bottle each time
questions.expected: Refilling a glass bottle instead of throwing it away
questions.memo: Reusing means using something again instead of discarding it, like refilling a bottle.

questions.question: Turning used materials, like paper or plastic, into new products is called ____.
questions.memo: Recycling processes used materials into new goods.

questions.question: Why should we use goods and services efficiently?
options: Resources are limited, so we should not waste them
Waste is good for the planet
questions.expected: Resources are limited, so we should not waste them
questions.memo: Because resources are scarce, using them efficiently helps them go further and protects the environment.

questions.question: Switching off lights when you leave a room is a way of using electricity efficiently.
questions.memo: Turning off unused lights avoids waste, an everyday example of efficient resource use.

questions.question: Which action reduces waste in a household?
questions.memo: Reusing and recycling cut down on waste and save resources.

questions.question: Using something again instead of throwing it away is called ____.
questions.memo: Reusing extends a product's life and reduces waste.

questions.question: How does using resources wisely help the community?
options: It saves money and protects the environment
questions.expected: It saves money and protects the environment
questions.memo: Wise use saves money and keeps the environment cleaner for everyone.

questions.question: Buying only what you need is a way of using resources efficiently.
questions.memo: Buying only what you need avoids waste and uses money and resources efficiently.

questions.question: Which is the best example of recycling?
options: Collecting plastic bottles so they can be made into new products
questions.expected: Collecting plastic bottles so they can be made into new products
questions.memo: Recycling collects used materials to make new products instead of throwing them away.

questions.question: A family uses both sides of paper before recycling it. This shows ____.
questions.memo: Using both sides then recycling gets maximum use from the paper — efficient resource use.

questions.question: Wasting goods and services makes no difference because resources are unlimited.
questions.memo: Resources are limited, so wasting them does matter — it raises costs and harms the environment.

questions.question: Using less water by fixing a leaking tap is an example of using a resource ____.
questions.memo: Fixing leaks avoids waste, which is efficient use of water.

questions.question: Which choice best protects limited resources for the future?
questions.memo: 'Reduce, reuse, recycle' keeps resources in use longer and protects them for the future.

questions.question: Reusing and recycling can both save money and reduce waste.
questions.memo: They cut spending on new goods and reduce the rubbish sent to landfills.

questions.question: Put the 'waste hierarchy' in order from best to last choice for the environment.

items.text: Reduce (use less in the first place)

questions.memo: Best to worst for the environment: reduce, then reuse, then recycle, and only then throw away.

questions.question: Sort each action into 'Uses resources wisely' or 'Wastes resources'.

items.text: Throwing away food that is still good

questions.expected: Recycling and switching off lights are wise; running taps and wasting food are wasteful.
questions.memo: Wise use avoids waste and stretches limited resources; careless habits waste them.

questions.question: Why is it important to use goods and services efficiently and effectively?
options: Because resources are limited and should not be wasted
To create as much rubbish as possible
questions.expected: Because resources are limited and should not be wasted
questions.memo: Efficient and effective use respects the limited nature of resources and benefits people and the planet.

questions.question: Reusing and recycling both help reduce waste and save resources.
questions.memo: Reusing and recycling keep materials in use, cutting waste and saving limited resources.

EMS.G7.E4.A1.title: Causes of socio-economic imbalances
EMS.G7.E4.A1.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T3) — Inequality and poverty: Causes of socio-economic imbalances.
EMS.G7.E4.A1.recovery_strategy: Inequality has roots in history, unequal access and unemployment.

questions.question: What does 'inequality' mean in an economy?
options: Some people have much more wealth and opportunity than others
questions.expected: Some people have much more wealth and opportunity than others
questions.memo: Inequality means wealth, income and opportunities are shared unevenly among people.

questions.question: Unemployment can be a cause of poverty and inequality.
questions.memo: When people cannot find work, they earn no income, which deepens poverty and inequality.

questions.question: Which of these is a cause of socio-economic imbalance in South Africa?
options: Unequal access to education in the past
questions.expected: Unequal access to education in the past
questions.memo: Past unequal access to education and opportunities is a major cause of today's imbalances.

questions.question: When wealth and income are shared very unevenly, we call this ____.
questions.memo: Inequality is the uneven sharing of wealth, income and opportunity.

questions.question: Which factor can increase poverty?
questions.memo: When there are few jobs, more people are without income, which increases poverty.

questions.question: South Africa's history has contributed to its present-day inequality.
questions.memo: Past policies created unequal access to land, education and jobs, shaping inequality today.

questions.question: Poverty is best described as ____.
options: not having enough income to meet basic needs
questions.expected: not having enough income to meet basic needs
questions.memo: Poverty means lacking the income or resources to meet basic needs like food and shelter.

questions.question: A lack of jobs, or ____, is a major cause of poverty.
questions.memo: Unemployment leaves people without income, a key driver of poverty.

questions.question: Which of these would most likely reduce inequality over time?
options: Better access to quality education and skills
questions.expected: Better access to quality education and skills
questions.memo: Education and skills open up better jobs and income, reducing inequality over time.

questions.question: Inequality means everyone in a country earns the same income.
questions.memo: Inequality is the opposite — incomes and wealth are shared very unevenly.

questions.question: Which is a social effect of poverty?
options: Poor access to healthcare and education
questions.expected: Poor access to healthcare and education
questions.memo: Poverty often limits access to healthcare and education, deepening disadvantage.

questions.question: Why is unemployment such a serious cause of poverty?
options: Without a job, a person has little or no income
It has no link to poverty
questions.expected: Without a job, a person has little or no income
questions.memo: No job usually means no regular income, which makes meeting basic needs very hard.

questions.question: Access to land, education and jobs affects how wealth is shared in a country.
questions.memo: Who can access land, education and jobs strongly shapes the distribution of wealth.

questions.question: People who cannot meet their basic needs are living in ____.
questions.memo: Poverty is the state of not being able to meet basic needs.

questions.question: Which combination of factors most increases socio-economic imbalance?
options: High unemployment and unequal access to education
questions.expected: High unemployment and unequal access to education
questions.memo: Together, joblessness and unequal education widen the gap between rich and poor.

questions.question: Reducing unemployment can help reduce poverty and inequality.
questions.memo: More jobs mean more incomes, which lifts people out of poverty and narrows inequality.

questions.question: Put this chain from cause to effect in order.

items.text: A person cannot find a job
They earn little or no income
They struggle to meet basic needs

questions.memo: No job → no income → can't meet basic needs → poverty.

questions.question: Sort each item into 'Cause of inequality' or 'Way to reduce inequality'.
questions.expected: Unemployment and unequal access cause inequality; education and job creation reduce it.
questions.memo: Lack of jobs and unequal access drive inequality; education and job creation help close the gap.

questions.question: Which statement is correct?
options: Inequality and poverty have causes such as unemployment and unequal access to education
questions.expected: Inequality and poverty have causes such as unemployment and unequal access to education
questions.memo: Joblessness and unequal access to education and opportunity are key causes of poverty and inequality.

questions.question: Unemployment is one of the major causes of poverty.
questions.memo: Without jobs, people earn little or no income, which is a leading cause of poverty.

EMS.G7.E4.A2.title: Urban and rural challenges
EMS.G7.E4.A2.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T3) — Inequality and poverty: Urban and rural challenges.
EMS.G7.E4.A2.recovery_strategy: Cities and rural areas face different versions of poverty and inequality.

questions.question: What is an 'urban' area?
options: A town or city with many people and buildings
questions.expected: A town or city with many people and buildings
questions.memo: Urban areas are towns and cities with dense populations, businesses and infrastructure.

questions.question: A rural area is usually a countryside or farming area with fewer people.
questions.memo: Rural areas have smaller, more spread-out populations, often based on farming.

questions.question: Which is a common challenge in urban (city) areas?
questions.memo: Cities often face overcrowding, informal settlements and pressure on services.

questions.question: A countryside or farming area with fewer people is called a ____ area.
questions.memo: Rural areas are the countryside, with fewer people and more farming.

questions.question: Which is a common challenge in rural areas?
options: Long distances to clinics, schools and jobs
questions.expected: Long distances to clinics, schools and jobs
questions.memo: Rural areas often have fewer services nearby, so people travel far for clinics, schools and work.

questions.question: People sometimes move from rural areas to cities to look for work.
questions.memo: Many people migrate to cities hoping to find jobs and better services.

questions.question: Why might someone leave a rural area for a city?
options: To get further from all services
questions.memo: Cities usually offer more jobs and services, which pulls people from rural areas.

questions.question: When too many people crowd into a city area, this is called ____.
questions.memo: Overcrowding happens when an area has more people than its housing and services can handle.

questions.question: Which challenge is more typical of rural areas than cities?
questions.memo: Rural areas usually have fewer services close by, unlike crowded cities.

questions.question: Both urban and rural areas can experience poverty, just in different ways.
questions.memo: Poverty exists in cities (e.g. informal settlements) and rural areas (e.g. few jobs) in different forms.

questions.question: An informal settlement (shacks without proper services) is most associated with which challenge?
questions.memo: Informal settlements often form when cities grow faster than housing and services can keep up.

questions.question: Which is a way to improve life in rural areas?
options: Building clinics, schools and roads closer to people
questions.expected: Building clinics, schools and roads closer to people
questions.memo: Bringing services and infrastructure closer reduces the distance challenge in rural areas.

questions.question: Cities never face any challenges because they have many services.
questions.memo: Cities face their own challenges like overcrowding, informal settlements and traffic.

questions.question: Moving from the countryside to the city is sometimes called ____ to the city.
questions.memo: Migration to cities is the movement of people from rural to urban areas, often for work.

questions.question: Which statement best compares urban and rural challenges?
options: Cities struggle with overcrowding; rural areas struggle with distance to services
questions.expected: Cities struggle with overcrowding; rural areas struggle with distance to services
questions.memo: Urban challenges centre on overcrowding; rural challenges centre on access and distance.

questions.question: Improving services in both urban and rural areas can help reduce poverty.
questions.memo: Better services everywhere — health, education, jobs — help reduce poverty across the country.

questions.question: Put the steps of rural-to-urban migration in order.

items.text: Few jobs are available in the rural area
A person decides to move to the city
They search for work in the city
The city's housing and services come under pressure

questions.memo: Few rural jobs push people to the city, where the search for work adds pressure to housing and services.

questions.question: Sort each challenge into 'Mainly urban' or 'Mainly rural'.

items.text: Long travel to the nearest clinic

questions.expected: Overcrowding and traffic are urban; distance to clinics and few jobs are rural.
questions.memo: Urban areas crowd up; rural areas are spread out with services far away.

questions.question: Which statement is correct?
options: Urban and rural areas face different challenges linked to poverty and inequality
Urban and rural areas are exactly the same
questions.expected: Urban and rural areas face different challenges linked to poverty and inequality
questions.memo: Both areas face poverty and inequality, but the specific challenges differ.

questions.question: Urban and rural areas often face different kinds of challenges.
questions.memo: Cities tend to struggle with overcrowding, while rural areas struggle with distance to services.

EMS.G7.E4.A3.title: Fighting inequality with education and jobs
EMS.G7.E4.A3.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T3) — Inequality and poverty: Fighting inequality with education and jobs.
EMS.G7.E4.A3.recovery_strategy: Skills and jobs are the long-term tools against inequality.

questions.question: How does education help fight inequality?
options: It gives people skills to get better jobs and income
questions.expected: It gives people skills to get better jobs and income
questions.memo: Education builds skills that open doors to better-paid work, helping reduce inequality.

questions.question: Creating sustainable jobs helps reduce poverty over the long term.
questions.memo: Lasting jobs provide steady incomes, which lift people out of poverty over time.

questions.question: What does a 'sustainable' job mean?
options: A job that can last and keep providing income over time
A job that ends in one day
A job that harms the environment
questions.expected: A job that can last and keep providing income over time
questions.memo: A sustainable job lasts and keeps producing income without quickly disappearing.

questions.question: Gaining skills and knowledge through ____ improves a person's chances of getting a good job.
questions.memo: Education builds the skills employers want, improving job prospects.

questions.question: Which is the best long-term way to reduce inequality?
options: Investing in education and creating jobs
Handing out money once and stopping
questions.expected: Investing in education and creating jobs
questions.memo: Education and job creation tackle the roots of inequality and last over time.

questions.question: Skills training can help unemployed people find work.
questions.memo: Training gives people marketable skills, improving their chances of employment.

questions.question: Why are skills important for fighting injustice and inequality?
options: Skilled people can access better opportunities and income
Skills only matter to the rich
questions.expected: Skilled people can access better opportunities and income
questions.memo: Skills widen access to opportunity and income, which helps reduce unfair gaps.

questions.question: A job that keeps providing income over a long time is called a ____ job.
questions.memo: Sustainable jobs last and keep supporting people, unlike once-off work.

questions.question: Which combination most helps reduce inequality?
options: Good education plus sustainable job creation
questions.expected: Good education plus sustainable job creation
questions.memo: Education and lasting jobs together attack inequality at its source.

questions.question: Education and skills only benefit individuals, never the wider community.
questions.memo: Educated, skilled people contribute to the whole economy and community, not just themselves.

questions.question: A young person completes training and starts a steady job. How does this help fight inequality?
options: They earn an income and improve their living standard
questions.expected: They earn an income and improve their living standard
questions.memo: A steady income from a job raises living standards and narrows the gap.

questions.question: Which is an example of investing in people to fight inequality?
options: Providing free schooling and skills programmes
questions.expected: Providing free schooling and skills programmes
questions.memo: Schooling and skills programmes build people's abilities to earn and progress.

questions.question: More skilled workers can help an economy grow and create more jobs.
questions.memo: A skilled workforce boosts productivity and growth, which can create further jobs.

questions.question: Education and skills help fight inequality and ____.
questions.memo: Education and skills give people fairer access to opportunity, fighting inequality and injustice.

questions.question: Which statement best explains the link between education and income?
options: More education often leads to better-paying jobs
Income has nothing to do with education
questions.expected: More education often leads to better-paying jobs
questions.memo: On average, more education and skills lead to higher-paying work.

questions.question: Fighting inequality usually needs both education and the creation of jobs.
questions.memo: Education builds skills, and jobs put them to use — both are needed to reduce inequality.

questions.question: Put the path out of poverty through education and work in order.

items.text: A learner gets a good education
They earn an income and improve their living standard

questions.memo: Education → skills → a lasting job → income and a better living standard.

questions.question: Sort each action into 'Helps fight inequality' or 'Does not help'.
questions.expected: Training and job creation help; closing schools and cutting education do not.
questions.memo: Education and job creation reduce inequality; removing them makes it worse.

questions.question: Which statement is correct?
options: Education, skills and sustainable jobs help fight inequality and injustice
Only money handouts can ever help
Education has no role in fighting inequality
questions.expected: Education, skills and sustainable jobs help fight inequality and injustice
questions.memo: Building education, skills and lasting jobs is a powerful long-term way to reduce inequality.

questions.question: Education and sustainable jobs together help reduce inequality.
questions.memo: Education builds skills and jobs provide income — together they narrow the gap.

EMS.G7.E5.A1.title: Inputs and outputs
EMS.G7.E5.A1.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T4) — The production process: Inputs and outputs.
EMS.G7.E5.A1.recovery_strategy: Production turns inputs (materials, labour) into outputs (goods/services).

questions.question: What is 'production'?
options: Turning inputs into goods and services (outputs)
questions.expected: Turning inputs into goods and services (outputs)
questions.memo: Production is the process of using inputs to create outputs — goods and services.

questions.question: Inputs are the resources used to make a product.
questions.memo: Inputs are the materials, labour and tools that go into making a good or service.

questions.question: Which of these is an input for baking bread?
questions.memo: Flour is an input used to make bread; the finished loaf is the output.

questions.question: The finished good or service that comes out of production is called the ____.
questions.memo: Outputs are the finished goods and services produced from inputs.

questions.question: In making a wooden table, which is the output?
questions.memo: The table is the finished product (output); wood, nails and tools are inputs.

questions.question: Labour (people working) is one of the inputs in production.
questions.memo: Labour is a key input — production needs people's work as well as materials.

questions.question: Which list shows only inputs for making a chair?
questions.memo: Wood, nails and labour are inputs; the finished chair is the output.

questions.question: The resources that go into making a product are called ____.
questions.memo: Inputs are the materials, labour and tools used in production.

questions.question: Why is the sustainable use of resources important in production?
options: So resources are not used up and are kept for the future
questions.expected: So resources are not used up and are kept for the future
questions.memo: Sustainable use means producing without exhausting resources, protecting future supply.

questions.question: Production converts inputs into outputs.
questions.memo: The whole point of production is to transform inputs into useful outputs.

questions.question: A bakery uses flour, water, an oven and a baker's work to make bread. The bread is the ____.
questions.memo: The bread is the finished product — the output — created from the inputs.

questions.question: Which best describes the production process?
options: Inputs are combined and changed into outputs
Outputs are turned back into inputs
questions.expected: Inputs are combined and changed into outputs
questions.memo: Production combines and transforms inputs into finished outputs.

questions.question: Using resources carefully so they last is part of sustainable production.
questions.memo: Sustainable production uses resources carefully so they remain available in future.

questions.question: In production, inputs are changed into ____.
questions.memo: Production changes inputs into outputs — the finished goods and services.

questions.question: Which is an example of an output?
options: A finished pair of shoes ready to sell
The leather used to make them
questions.expected: A finished pair of shoes ready to sell
questions.memo: The finished shoes are the output; leather, machines and labour are inputs.

questions.question: Inputs and outputs are exactly the same thing.
questions.memo: Inputs go into production; outputs come out of it — they are different stages.

questions.question: Put the production of a loaf of bread in order.

items.text: Bake the dough in an oven
Produce the output: a finished loaf

questions.memo: Production moves from gathering inputs, through processing, to the finished output.

questions.question: Sort each item into 'Input' or 'Output' for a furniture maker.
questions.expected: Wood and labour are inputs; the wardrobe and table are outputs.
questions.memo: Inputs go in (wood, labour); outputs come out (finished furniture).

questions.question: Which statement is correct?
options: Production turns inputs into outputs, and resources should be used sustainably
questions.expected: Production turns inputs into outputs, and resources should be used sustainably
questions.memo: Production transforms inputs into outputs, and doing it sustainably protects future resources.

questions.question: During production, inputs are changed into outputs.
questions.memo: Production transforms inputs (materials, labour) into finished outputs.

EMS.G7.E5.A2.title: Economic growth and productivity
EMS.G7.E5.A2.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T4) — The production process: Economic growth and productivity.
EMS.G7.E5.A2.recovery_strategy: Productivity = getting more output from the same inputs; it drives growth.

questions.question: What is economic growth?
options: An increase in the goods and services a country produces
questions.expected: An increase in the goods and services a country produces
questions.memo: Economic growth means a country produces more goods and services over time.

questions.question: Productivity means producing more output from the same amount of inputs.
questions.memo: Productivity rises when you get more output without using more inputs.

questions.question: If a worker makes 10 chairs a day instead of 5 using the same tools, their productivity has ____.
questions.memo: Producing more output (10 instead of 5) from the same inputs means productivity has increased.

questions.question: An increase in the total goods and services a country produces is called economic ____.
questions.memo: Economic growth is a rise in a country's total production over time.

questions.question: How does higher productivity help economic growth?
options: More is produced, so the economy can grow
questions.expected: More is produced, so the economy can grow
questions.memo: When productivity rises, more goods and services are made, which supports economic growth.

questions.question: Producing more output without using extra resources is good for both the business and the economy.
questions.memo: Higher productivity means more output at the same cost, benefiting businesses and the wider economy.

questions.question: Which is an example of improved productivity?
options: A bakery bakes more bread per hour after training staff
A bakery closes for a week
A bakery bakes less each day
questions.expected: A bakery bakes more bread per hour after training staff
questions.memo: Baking more per hour with the same inputs is a clear productivity gain.

questions.question: Getting more output from the same inputs is called higher ____.
questions.memo: Productivity measures how much output you get from your inputs.

questions.question: Why do countries want economic growth?
options: It can create jobs and improve living standards
questions.expected: It can create jobs and improve living standards
questions.memo: Growth tends to create jobs and raise incomes, improving living standards.

questions.question: Productivity and economic growth are completely unrelated.
questions.memo: They are closely linked — rising productivity is a major driver of economic growth.

questions.question: Which would most likely raise a factory's productivity?
options: Training workers and using better machines
questions.expected: Training workers and using better machines
questions.memo: Better skills and equipment let workers produce more from the same inputs.

questions.question: A country's production rises year after year. This shows ____.
questions.memo: Steadily rising production over time is economic growth.

questions.question: Improving productivity can help a business produce more without spending more on inputs.
questions.memo: Higher productivity squeezes more output from the same inputs, so output rises without extra input cost.

questions.question: When productivity rises across many businesses, the whole economy can experience ____.
questions.memo: Widespread productivity gains lift total production, driving economic growth.

questions.question: Which statement about growth and productivity is correct?
options: Productivity has no link to output
questions.memo: Producing more from the same inputs (productivity) helps the economy grow.

questions.question: Economic growth usually means a country is producing more than before.
questions.memo: Growth is measured by an increase in the goods and services produced.

questions.question: Put this chain showing how training leads to growth in order.

items.text: They produce more from the same inputs

questions.memo: Training → higher productivity → more output → economic growth.

questions.question: Sort each example into 'Higher productivity' or 'Lower productivity'.

items.text: Making 12 items an hour instead of 8

questions.expected: More output per hour and better training raise productivity; breakdowns and waste lower it.
questions.memo: Productivity rises when output per input goes up; it falls with waste and breakdowns.

questions.question: Which statement is correct?
options: Productivity is output from given inputs; growth is producing more over time
Productivity and growth mean producing less
Growth has nothing to do with production
questions.expected: Productivity is output from given inputs; growth is producing more over time
questions.memo: Productivity is how much you make from your inputs; economic growth is producing more over time.

questions.question: Higher productivity can support a country's economic growth.
questions.memo: Producing more from the same inputs lifts total output, which supports growth.

EMS.G7.E5.A3.title: Technology and sustainable resources
EMS.G7.E5.A3.description: The Economy (CAPS G7 T4) — The production process: Technology and sustainable resources.
EMS.G7.E5.A3.recovery_strategy: Technology lifts output; sustainability keeps resources for the future.

questions.question: How can technology improve production?
options: By helping produce more, faster, with less effort
questions.expected: By helping produce more, faster, with less effort
questions.memo: Technology (machines, computers, tools) raises output and speed while reducing effort.

questions.question: Machines and computers are examples of technology used in production.
questions.memo: Technology includes machines, computers and tools that help make goods and services.

questions.question: Using a tractor instead of digging by hand is an example of ____ improving productivity.
questions.memo: A tractor is technology that lets a farmer do far more work in less time.

questions.question: Tools, machines and computers used to produce goods and services are called ____.
questions.memo: Technology is the equipment and methods used to produce more efficiently.

questions.question: What does 'sustainable use of resources' mean?
options: Using resources so they are not used up and last for the future
Using everything up as fast as possible
questions.expected: Using resources so they are not used up and last for the future
questions.memo: Sustainable use protects resources so they remain available for future generations.

questions.question: Technology can sometimes help businesses use resources more efficiently.
questions.memo: Better technology can reduce waste and use materials and energy more efficiently.

questions.question: Why should production be sustainable?
options: So future generations still have resources to use
questions.expected: So future generations still have resources to use
questions.memo: Sustainable production keeps resources available for the future, not just today.

questions.question: Using resources carefully so they last for the future is called ____ use.
questions.memo: Sustainable use means using resources in a way that keeps them available over time.

questions.question: Which is a benefit of technology in production?
options: Goods can be made faster and in larger amounts
questions.expected: Goods can be made faster and in larger amounts
questions.memo: Technology speeds up production and increases the amount that can be made.

questions.question: Producing without thinking about resources can harm the environment and future supply.
questions.memo: Careless production can damage the environment and use up resources needed in future.

questions.question: A factory installs energy-saving machines that use less electricity. This supports ____.
questions.memo: Energy-saving machines use fewer resources, supporting sustainable, efficient production.

questions.question: How does technology contribute to economic growth?
options: It raises productivity, so more is produced
questions.expected: It raises productivity, so more is produced
questions.memo: By boosting productivity, technology increases output and supports economic growth.

questions.question: Sustainable production and technology can work together to produce more while protecting resources.
questions.memo: Good technology can raise output while using resources more carefully — combining growth and sustainability.

questions.question: Better ____ can help a business produce more goods in less time.
questions.memo: Improved technology raises how much can be produced in a given time.

questions.question: Which statement best links technology, productivity and growth?
options: Technology raises productivity, which supports economic growth
Growth needs no technology or productivity
questions.expected: Technology raises productivity, which supports economic growth
questions.memo: Technology improves productivity, and higher productivity drives economic growth.

questions.question: Protecting resources while producing is bad for the future.
questions.memo: Protecting resources is good for the future — it keeps them available for later generations.

questions.question: Put this chain from technology to growth in order.

items.text: Workers produce more in less time

questions.memo: Better technology → more output per worker → higher productivity → economic growth.

questions.question: Sort each action into 'Sustainable' or 'Unsustainable' use of resources.

items.text: Using up resources with no plan

questions.expected: Energy-saving and recycling are sustainable; dumping waste and careless use are unsustainable.
questions.memo: Sustainable use saves resources and protects the environment; unsustainable use wastes and pollutes.

questions.question: Which statement is correct?
options: Technology can raise productivity and growth, and resources should be used sustainably
questions.expected: Technology can raise productivity and growth, and resources should be used sustainably
questions.memo: Technology boosts productivity and growth, while sustainable use protects resources for the future.

questions.question: Technology can raise productivity while resources are still used sustainably.
questions.memo: Good technology can increase output and use resources more carefully at the same time.

EMS.G7.F1.A1.title: Capital, assets and liabilities
EMS.G7.F1.A1.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G7 T2) — Accounting concepts: Capital, assets and liabilities.
EMS.G7.F1.A1.recovery_strategy: Assets = what you own; liabilities = what you owe; capital = the owner's stake.

questions.question: What are 'assets'?
options: Things a person or business owns
questions.expected: Things a person or business owns
questions.memo: Assets are the things you own that have value, like cash, equipment or a vehicle.

questions.question: What is a 'liability'?
options: Money a person or business owes to others
questions.expected: Money a person or business owes to others
questions.memo: A liability is a debt — money you owe to someone else, like a loan.

questions.question: What does 'capital' mean for a business owner?
options: The money or assets the owner puts into the business
questions.expected: The money or assets the owner puts into the business
questions.memo: Capital is the owner's own contribution of money or assets to start or run the business.

questions.question: Which of these is an asset?
options: A delivery van the business owns
A loan the business must repay
questions.expected: A delivery van the business owns
questions.memo: A van the business owns is an asset; the others are debts (liabilities).

questions.question: Which of these is a liability?
options: A bank loan that must be repaid
questions.expected: A bank loan that must be repaid
questions.memo: A loan to repay is a liability; cash, computers and stock are assets.

questions.question: If a business owns a building worth R500 000, the building is recorded as a(n) ____.
questions.memo: Something valuable the business owns, like a building, is an asset.

questions.question: Mr Khumalo starts a shop using R20 000 of his own savings. That R20 000 is his ____.
questions.memo: Money the owner puts into the business is the owner's capital.

questions.question: Which list contains only assets?
questions.memo: Cash, a vehicle and equipment are all owned items (assets).

questions.question: Why is it useful to know your assets and liabilities?
options: To see what you own and what you owe
questions.expected: To see what you own and what you owe
questions.memo: Knowing assets and liabilities shows your true financial position — what you own versus what you owe.

questions.question: A friend lends a business R5 000. For the business, this R5 000 is a(n) ____.
questions.memo: Borrowed money must be repaid, so it is a liability for the business.

questions.question: Assets are things you own; liabilities are things you owe.
questions.memo: This is the key distinction: assets = owned, liabilities = owed.

questions.question: Capital is money the owner contributes to the business.
questions.memo: Capital is the owner's own investment of money or assets into the business.

questions.question: A bank loan is an example of an asset.
questions.memo: A loan must be repaid, so it is a liability, not an asset.

questions.question: Cash in the bank is an asset of the business.
