questions.memo: Cash the business owns is one of its assets.

questions.question: Items a business owns, such as equipment and cash, are called ____.
questions.memo: Assets are the valuable things a business owns.

questions.question: Money a business owes to others is called a ____.
questions.memo: Liabilities are debts the business owes.

questions.question: The owner's own money put into the business is called ____.
questions.memo: Capital is the owner's contribution to the business.

questions.question: A vehicle the business owns is an example of an ____.
questions.memo: An owned vehicle is an asset.

questions.question: Sort each item into 'Asset' or 'Liability'.
questions.expected: Cash and the vehicle are assets; the loan and money owed are liabilities.
questions.memo: Owned items are assets; debts owed to others are liabilities.

questions.question: Put these steps of starting a small business in order.

items.text: The business buys assets like equipment
The business may take a loan (a liability) if needed
The owner keeps records of what is owned and owed

questions.memo: Capital comes first, then assets are bought, loans may be taken, and records track it all.

EMS.G7.F1.A2.title: Income, expenses, profit and loss
EMS.G7.F1.A2.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G7 T2) — Accounting concepts: Income, expenses, profit and loss.
EMS.G7.F1.A2.recovery_strategy: Profit = income minus expenses; a loss is when expenses win.

questions.question: What is 'income'?
options: Money coming in to a person or business
questions.expected: Money coming in to a person or business
questions.memo: Income is money received, such as sales, wages or interest.

questions.question: What is an 'expense'?
options: Money paid out to run a business or household
questions.expected: Money paid out to run a business or household
questions.memo: Expenses are the costs paid out, like rent, wages and electricity.

questions.question: How do you work out profit?
questions.memo: Profit = income − expenses. If income is greater, you make a profit.

questions.question: When does a business make a loss?
options: When expenses are greater than income
When income is greater than expenses
questions.expected: When expenses are greater than income
questions.memo: A loss happens when expenses exceed income — more money goes out than comes in.

questions.question: A stall earns R800 and spends R500. What is the profit?
questions.memo: Profit = R800 − R500 = R300.

questions.question: A stall earns R400 and spends R600. What is the result?
questions.memo: Expenses (R600) are more than income (R400), so there is a loss of R200.

questions.question: Which of these is income for a tuckshop?
questions.memo: Sales of snacks bring money in, so that is income; the rest are expenses.

questions.question: Which of these is an expense for a tuckshop?
questions.memo: Paying for stock is money going out — an expense.

questions.question: Why do businesses want income to be higher than expenses?
questions.memo: When income beats expenses, the business earns a profit.

questions.question: If income exactly equals expenses, the business ____.
questions.memo: When income equals expenses, the business breaks even — neither profit nor loss.

questions.question: Profit is what is left when income is greater than expenses.
questions.memo: Profit is the positive difference: income minus expenses.

questions.question: A loss happens when income is greater than expenses.
questions.memo: A loss happens when expenses are greater than income, not the other way around.

questions.question: Rent and wages are examples of expenses.
questions.memo: Rent and wages are costs paid out, so they are expenses.

questions.question: Money received from selling goods is income.
questions.memo: Sales bring money in, which is income.

questions.question: Money received by a business is called ____.
questions.memo: Income is money flowing into the business.

questions.question: Money paid out to run a business is called ____.
questions.memo: Expenses are the costs paid out.

questions.question: Profit is income ____ expenses.
questions.memo: Profit = income − expenses.

questions.question: When expenses are more than income, the business makes a ____.
questions.memo: More out than in means a loss.

questions.question: Sort each item into 'Income' or 'Expense'.
questions.expected: Sales and interest are income; rent and packaging are expenses.
questions.memo: Income is money in; expenses are money out.

questions.question: Put the steps of working out profit in order.

items.text: See if the result is a profit or a loss

questions.memo: Total income, total expenses, subtract, then check for profit or loss.

EMS.G7.F1.A3.title: Budgets, savings, banking and records
EMS.G7.F1.A3.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G7 T2) — Accounting concepts: Budgets, savings, banking and records.
EMS.G7.F1.A3.recovery_strategy: Records track money in and out; a budget plans it ahead.

questions.question: What is a budget?
options: A plan for expected income and expenses
A record of past sales only
questions.expected: A plan for expected income and expenses
questions.memo: A budget is a plan that estimates future income and expenses.

questions.question: What does it mean to 'save'?
options: To keep some money for later instead of spending it
questions.expected: To keep some money for later instead of spending it
questions.memo: Saving means setting money aside now to use in the future.

questions.question: Why do people and businesses keep financial records?
options: To track money coming in and going out
questions.expected: To track money coming in and going out
questions.memo: Records track income and expenses so you know your true financial position.

questions.question: What is a 'transaction'?
options: An exchange of money for goods or services
questions.expected: An exchange of money for goods or services
questions.memo: A transaction is any deal where money is exchanged for goods or services.

questions.question: Which is a benefit of having a budget?
options: It helps you plan and avoid overspending
It pays your bills for you
questions.expected: It helps you plan and avoid overspending
questions.memo: A budget helps you plan spending so you don't run out of money.

questions.question: Where do most people keep their savings safely?
questions.memo: A bank keeps savings safe and may pay interest.

questions.question: Keeping records helps a business to ____.
options: see whether it is making a profit or loss
questions.expected: see whether it is making a profit or loss
questions.memo: Good records show income and expenses, revealing profit or loss.

questions.question: Which of these is a transaction?
options: Buying a loaf of bread for R15
questions.expected: Buying a loaf of bread for R15
questions.memo: Exchanging R15 for bread is a transaction.

questions.question: Saving regularly, even small amounts, helps you to ____.
options: build up money for future needs
questions.expected: build up money for future needs
questions.memo: Regular saving grows a sum you can use for future needs or emergencies.

questions.question: A budget that plans to spend more than the income coming in is ____.
options: a problem, because it cannot balance
questions.expected: a problem, because it cannot balance
questions.memo: A budget should not plan to spend more than the income available, or it won't balance.

questions.question: A budget is a plan for future income and expenses.
questions.memo: Budgets plan ahead for the money expected to come in and go out.

questions.question: Saving means spending all your money immediately.
questions.memo: Saving is the opposite — keeping some money for later instead of spending it now.

questions.question: Banks can keep your money safe and sometimes pay interest.
questions.memo: Banks store money securely and may add interest to savings.

questions.question: Keeping financial records helps you understand your money.
questions.memo: Records show where money comes from and goes, helping you manage it.

questions.question: A plan for future income and expenses is called a ____.
questions.memo: A budget plans expected income and spending.

questions.question: Keeping money aside for the future is called ____.
questions.memo: Saving sets money aside for later use.

questions.question: An exchange of money for goods or services is a ____.
questions.memo: A transaction is any money-for-goods/services exchange.

questions.question: Writing down money received and paid out is called keeping ____.
questions.memo: Financial records track money in and out.

questions.question: Sort each item into 'Budgeting/Saving habit' or 'Poor money habit'.
questions.expected: Budgeting and saving are good habits; spending with no plan and keeping no records are poor habits.
questions.memo: Planning, saving and record-keeping are good habits; no plan and no records are poor habits.

questions.question: Put the steps of managing money in a sensible order.

items.text: Make a budget for the month
Record income and expenses as they happen
Check your records against your budget

questions.memo: Plan a budget, record actual money, save the surplus, then compare records with the plan.

EMS.G7.F2.A1.title: Personal income
EMS.G7.F2.A1.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G7 T2) — Income and expenses: Personal income.
EMS.G7.F2.A1.recovery_strategy: Income is money coming in — wages, salary, pocket money, interest.

questions.question: What is personal income?
questions.memo: Personal income is the money an individual receives, such as wages or pocket money.

questions.question: Which of these is a type of personal income?
questions.memo: A salary is money received for work — personal income; the others are money paid out.

questions.question: What is a 'wage'?
options: Money paid for work, often by the hour or week
questions.expected: Money paid for work, often by the hour or week
questions.memo: A wage is payment for work, often calculated hourly, daily or weekly.

questions.question: Interest earned on money in a savings account is a form of ____.
questions.memo: Interest is money the bank pays you, so it is income.

questions.question: Which is the difference between a salary and a wage?
options: A salary is usually a fixed monthly amount; a wage is often paid hourly or weekly
A salary is paid hourly; a wage is monthly
A wage is never payment for work
questions.expected: A salary is usually a fixed monthly amount; a wage is often paid hourly or weekly
questions.memo: Salaries are typically fixed monthly pay; wages are often hourly or weekly.

questions.question: Pocket money a learner receives is an example of their ____.
questions.memo: Pocket money is money received, so it is personal income.

questions.question: Which of these would increase a person's income?
questions.memo: A part-time job brings in more money, increasing income.

questions.question: A person who is self-employed earns income from ____.
questions.memo: Self-employed people earn income from running their own business.

questions.question: Which is NOT a source of personal income?
questions.memo: Paying for groceries is spending (an expense), not income.

questions.question: Why is it useful to know all your sources of income?
options: To plan how much you can spend and save
questions.expected: To plan how much you can spend and save
questions.memo: Knowing your income lets you plan spending and saving sensibly.

questions.question: A salary is a form of personal income.
questions.memo: A salary is money received for work, so it is personal income.

questions.question: Pocket money received by a learner is an expense.
questions.memo: Pocket money is money received, so it is income, not an expense.

questions.question: Interest paid to you by a bank is a type of income.
questions.memo: Interest the bank pays you adds to your income.

questions.question: People can have more than one source of income.
questions.memo: A person might earn a salary and also receive interest or run a side business.

questions.question: Money a person receives is called personal ____.
questions.memo: Personal income is the money an individual receives.

questions.question: Money paid for work, often per hour or week, is a ____.
questions.memo: A wage is payment for work, usually hourly or weekly.

questions.question: A fixed monthly payment for a job is usually called a ____.
questions.memo: A salary is typically a fixed monthly amount.

questions.question: Money the bank pays you on your savings is called ____.
questions.memo: Interest is what the bank pays you for keeping money with them.

questions.question: Sort each item into 'Personal income' or 'Not income'.

items.text: A monthly rent payment you make

questions.expected: Wages and interest are income; paying for airtime or rent is spending.
questions.memo: Income is money received; payments you make are expenses, not income.

questions.question: Put these income-earning steps in order for a learner doing a holiday job.

items.text: The learner finds a holiday job
They decide how much to spend and save

questions.memo: Earning income: get the job, do the work, receive the wage, then plan spending and saving.

EMS.G7.F2.A2.title: Personal expenses and net worth
EMS.G7.F2.A2.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G7 T2) — Income and expenses: Personal expenses and net worth.
EMS.G7.F2.A2.recovery_strategy: Net worth = what you own minus what you owe.

questions.question: What is a personal expense?
options: Something a person owns for free
questions.memo: A personal expense is money you pay out, like food, transport or airtime.

questions.question: What does 'net worth' mean?
options: What you own minus what you owe
The money in your pocket only
questions.expected: What you own minus what you owe
questions.memo: Net worth = assets (what you own) − liabilities (what you owe).

questions.question: Which of these is a personal expense?
questions.memo: Buying lunch is spending money, so it is an expense.

questions.question: A person owns R5 000 in assets and owes R2 000. Their net worth is ____.
questions.memo: Net worth = R5 000 − R2 000 = R3 000.

questions.question: Which would increase a person's net worth?
questions.memo: More assets and less debt raise net worth.

questions.question: A statement listing what you own and owe to work out net worth is a personal statement of ____.
questions.memo: A statement of net worth lists assets and liabilities to find net worth.

questions.question: Which is a fixed expense (roughly the same each month)?
questions.memo: Rent is usually a fixed, regular monthly expense.

questions.question: Spending less than you earn helps you to ____.
questions.memo: Spending less than income lets you save, which builds net worth.

questions.question: Which list contains only personal expenses?
questions.memo: Transport, food and airtime are all things you pay for — expenses.

questions.question: If your expenses are higher than your income every month, you will likely ____.
questions.memo: Spending more than you earn forces you to borrow, building debt.

questions.question: A personal expense is money you spend.
questions.memo: Expenses are money paid out.

questions.question: Net worth is what you own minus what you owe.
questions.memo: Net worth = assets − liabilities.

questions.question: Reducing your debt can increase your net worth.
questions.memo: Lower liabilities raise net worth, since net worth = assets − liabilities.

questions.question: Buying food is a form of personal income.
questions.memo: Buying food is spending money, which is an expense, not income.

questions.question: Money a person spends is called a personal ____.
questions.memo: Personal expenses are the money you pay out.

questions.question: What you own minus what you owe is your ____ worth.
questions.memo: Net worth = assets − liabilities.

questions.question: An expense that stays about the same each month, like rent, is a ____ expense.
questions.memo: Fixed expenses recur at roughly the same amount each period.

questions.question: To build savings, you should spend ____ than you earn.
questions.memo: Spending less than you earn leaves money to save.

questions.question: Sort each item into 'Asset (owned)' or 'Liability (owed)' for working out net worth.
questions.expected: Savings and the bicycle are assets; money owed to a friend and the phone account are liabilities.
questions.memo: Net worth uses assets (owned) minus liabilities (owed).

questions.question: Put the steps of working out personal net worth in order.

items.text: Subtract what you owe from what you own
The answer is your net worth

questions.memo: List assets, list liabilities, subtract, and the result is net worth.

EMS.G7.F2.A3.title: Business income and expenses
EMS.G7.F2.A3.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G7 T2) — Income and expenses: Business income and expenses.
EMS.G7.F2.A3.recovery_strategy: Businesses have their own income and expenses, just on a bigger scale.

questions.question: What is the main source of income for most businesses?
options: Money from selling goods or services
questions.expected: Money from selling goods or services
questions.memo: Most business income comes from selling goods or services to customers.

questions.question: Which of these is a business expense?
questions.memo: Wages are money paid out by the business — an expense.

questions.question: Why might a business put some money into savings or investments?
options: To grow money and prepare for future needs
questions.expected: To grow money and prepare for future needs
questions.memo: Saving or investing helps a business prepare for the future and grow its money.

questions.question: Which is a typical business income?
questions.memo: Fees charged to customers bring money in — income.

questions.question: Which is a typical business expense?
questions.memo: Rent is money the business pays out — an expense.

questions.question: A business earns R10 000 from sales and pays R7 000 in expenses. It made a ____.
Investing business profits wisely can help the business to ____.
questions.memo: Wisely invested profits can fund growth and future stability.

questions.question: Which would reduce a business's profit?
questions.memo: Rising expenses eat into profit; higher sales or lower costs would raise it.

questions.question: Why must a business track both income and expenses?
options: To know whether it is making a profit
questions.expected: To know whether it is making a profit
questions.memo: Tracking both shows whether income beats expenses — that is, whether there is profit.

questions.question: A business that always spends more than it earns will eventually ____.
questions.memo: Persistently spending more than you earn leads to losses and financial trouble.

questions.question: Selling goods and services is the main income for most businesses.
questions.memo: Sales of goods and services are the main income source for businesses.

questions.question: Wages and rent are examples of business expenses.
questions.memo: Wages and rent are costs paid out by the business — expenses.

questions.question: Businesses can also save and invest some of their money.
questions.memo: Businesses, like people, can save and invest for future needs and growth.

questions.question: A business makes a profit when its expenses are higher than its income.
questions.memo: That is a loss. Profit occurs when income is higher than expenses.

questions.question: Most business income comes from ____ goods and services.
questions.memo: Selling goods and services brings money into the business.

questions.question: Wages, rent and electricity are business ____.
questions.memo: These are costs paid out — business expenses.

questions.question: Putting money aside to grow it for the future is called ____.
questions.memo: Investing puts money to work to grow it over time.

questions.question: A business makes a profit when income is ____ than expenses.
questions.memo: Profit happens when income is greater than expenses.

questions.question: Sort each item into 'Business income' or 'Business expense'.
questions.expected: Sales and service fees are income; wages and rent are expenses.
questions.memo: Money from customers is income; money paid to run the business is expense.

questions.question: Put the flow of money through a small business in order.

items.text: The business sells goods and earns income
It pays its expenses (wages, rent, stock)
It works out the profit that is left
It saves or invests some of the profit

questions.memo: Earn income, pay expenses, find the profit, then save or invest part of it.

EMS.G7.F3.A1.title: Personal budget
EMS.G7.F3.A1.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G7 T2) — Budgets: Personal budget.
EMS.G7.F3.A1.recovery_strategy: A budget makes sure spending does not beat income.

questions.question: What is a personal budget?
options: A plan of your expected income and spending
A record of a shop's sales
questions.expected: A plan of your expected income and spending
questions.memo: A personal budget plans how you will use your income on spending and saving.

questions.question: Why is a personal budget useful?
options: It helps you avoid spending more than you earn
questions.expected: It helps you avoid spending more than you earn
questions.memo: A budget keeps your spending within your income, helping you avoid debt.

questions.question: In a budget, what should you usually plan for first?
questions.memo: Budgets should cover essential needs before wants.

questions.question: If your income is R200 and you plan to spend R250, your budget ____.
questions.memo: Planning to spend more than you earn means the budget does not balance.

questions.question: A good personal budget leaves room to ____.
questions.memo: A healthy budget plans for saving, not just spending.

questions.question: Which is the income side of a personal budget?
options: Pocket money and a part-time wage
questions.expected: Pocket money and a part-time wage
questions.memo: Income is the money coming in, like pocket money and wages.

questions.question: Which is the expense side of a personal budget?
questions.memo: Expenses are what you plan to spend, like transport and food.

questions.question: If you stick to your budget, you are more likely to ____.
options: meet your needs and reach savings goals
questions.expected: meet your needs and reach savings goals
questions.memo: Sticking to a budget keeps spending in check and helps reach goals.

questions.question: What should you do if your planned expenses are more than your income?
options: Cut some spending or increase income
questions.expected: Cut some spending or increase income
questions.memo: To balance the budget, reduce spending or find more income.

questions.question: A learner budgets R100: R60 transport, R20 food, R20 saving. This budget ____.
questions.memo: R60 + R20 + R20 = R100, matching income, and it includes saving.

questions.question: A personal budget plans your income and spending.
questions.memo: A budget is a plan for income and spending.

questions.question: A budget should plan to spend more than you earn.
questions.memo: A good budget keeps spending within income, not above it.

questions.question: Including savings in your budget is a good habit.
questions.memo: Planning to save is part of a healthy budget.

questions.question: Needs should usually be budgeted for before wants.
questions.memo: Essential needs come before wants in a sensible budget.

questions.question: A plan of your income and spending is a personal ____.
questions.memo: A personal budget plans income and spending.

questions.question: In a budget, money coming in is your ____.
questions.memo: Income is the money coming in.

questions.question: In a budget, money you plan to spend is your ____.
questions.memo: Expenses are the planned spending.

questions.question: A balanced budget means spending is not ____ than income.
questions.memo: A balanced budget keeps spending at or below income.

questions.question: Sort each entry into the 'Income' or 'Expense' side of a personal budget.
questions.expected: Pocket money and wages are income; taxi fare and lunch are expenses.
questions.memo: Income is money in; expenses are planned money out.

questions.question: Put the steps of making a personal budget in order.

items.text: List your needs and their costs
Add any wants you can afford
Plan to save what is left over

questions.memo: Income first, then needs, then affordable wants, then saving.

EMS.G7.F3.A2.title: Business budget
EMS.G7.F3.A2.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G7 T2) — Budgets: Business budget.
EMS.G7.F3.A2.recovery_strategy: A business budget plans the firm's income and spending.

questions.question: What is a business budget?
options: A plan of a business's expected income and expenses
A record of personal pocket money
questions.expected: A plan of a business's expected income and expenses
questions.memo: A business budget plans the income and expenses the business expects.

questions.question: How is a business budget similar to a personal budget?
options: Both are only about pocket money
questions.memo: Both kinds of budget plan expected income and expenses, just at different scales.

questions.question: How is a business budget different from a personal one?
options: It deals with the business's income and costs, often larger
It is exactly the same in every way
It is only about one person's sweets
questions.expected: It deals with the business's income and costs, often larger
questions.memo: A business budget covers business income and costs, usually larger and more complex.

questions.question: Why does a business prepare a budget?
options: To plan ahead and control spending
questions.expected: To plan ahead and control spending
questions.memo: Budgets help a business plan and keep spending under control.

questions.question: Which would appear on the income side of a business budget?
questions.memo: Expected sales are income; rent, wages and electricity are expenses.

questions.question: Which would appear on the expense side of a business budget?
questions.memo: Buying stock is a planned cost — an expense.

questions.question: A business budget that plans for income to be higher than expenses expects a ____.
questions.memo: If planned income beats planned expenses, the budget expects a profit.

questions.question: If a business expects expenses to be higher than income, the budget warns of a possible ____.
questions.memo: Planned expenses above income signal a possible loss to address.

questions.question: How can a budget help a business avoid running out of money?
options: By planning income against expenses in advance
questions.expected: By planning income against expenses in advance
questions.memo: Planning ahead shows whether money will be enough to cover costs.

questions.question: A budget shows a shop expects R50 000 income and R45 000 expenses. The plan expects ____.
questions.memo: R50 000 − R45 000 = R5 000 expected profit.

questions.question: A business budget plans expected income and expenses.
questions.memo: Like a personal budget, it plans income and expenses, for the business.

questions.question: Budgets help businesses control spending and plan ahead.
questions.memo: Budgets are planning and control tools.

questions.question: A business budget only lists income and never expenses.
questions.memo: A budget lists both income and expenses so the business can plan.

questions.question: A business and a personal budget both plan for the future.
questions.memo: Both look ahead at expected income and spending.

questions.question: A plan of a business's income and expenses is a business ____.
questions.memo: A business budget plans the firm's income and expenses.

questions.question: Expected ____ appear on the income side of a business budget.
questions.memo: Sales are the main income a business plans for.

questions.question: Expected rent and wages appear on the ____ side of a business budget.
questions.memo: Rent and wages are planned costs — expenses.

questions.question: If planned income is more than planned expenses, the budget expects a ____.
questions.memo: Income above expenses means an expected profit.

questions.question: Sort each item into the 'Income' or 'Expense' side of a business budget.
questions.expected: Expected sales and fees are income; wages and rent are expenses.
questions.memo: Money the business expects to receive is income; money it expects to pay is expense.

questions.question: Put the steps of preparing a business budget in order.

items.text: Decide if a profit or loss is expected and adjust

questions.memo: Estimate income, estimate expenses, compare them, then plan for the expected profit or loss.

EMS.G7.F4.A1.title: Personal savings and its purpose
EMS.G7.F4.A1.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G7 T4) — Savings: Personal savings and its purpose.
EMS.G7.F4.A1.recovery_strategy: Saving = spending less than you earn and keeping the rest.

questions.question: What does it mean to save money?
options: To set money aside instead of spending it
To spend all of it now
questions.expected: To set money aside instead of spending it
questions.memo: Saving means keeping money for later rather than spending it now.

questions.question: Why is saving important?
options: It prepares you for future needs and emergencies
questions.expected: It prepares you for future needs and emergencies
questions.memo: Savings provide for future needs, goals and unexpected emergencies.

questions.question: Which is a good reason to save?
questions.memo: Saving lets you afford bigger or future purchases.

questions.question: An 'emergency fund' is money saved for ____.
questions.memo: An emergency fund covers surprise expenses like repairs or medical costs.

questions.question: Saving small amounts regularly will ____ over time.
options: add up to a larger sum
questions.expected: add up to a larger sum
questions.memo: Regular small savings build into a meaningful amount over time.

questions.question: Which habit helps you save?
questions.memo: Spending less than you earn leaves money to save.

questions.question: Saving for a goal, like a bicycle, is an example of ____.
questions.memo: Saving towards a specific goal gives your saving a clear purpose.

questions.question: Which is a benefit of having savings?
options: You can handle emergencies without borrowing
You will always be in debt
questions.expected: You can handle emergencies without borrowing
questions.memo: Savings let you cover surprises without taking on debt.

questions.question: If you spend everything you earn, you will have ____ for the future.
questions.memo: Spending all income leaves nothing to save for the future.

questions.question: Why might saving be difficult for some people?
options: Their income barely covers their needs
questions.expected: Their income barely covers their needs
questions.memo: When income only just meets basic needs, there is little or nothing left to save.

questions.question: Saving means keeping some money for later instead of spending it now.
questions.memo: Saving sets money aside for future use.

questions.question: Saving has no purpose and is a waste of money.
questions.memo: Saving prepares for future needs, goals and emergencies — it is very useful.

questions.question: Even small, regular savings can grow into a useful amount.
questions.memo: Saving small amounts often adds up over time.

questions.question: An emergency fund is money saved for unexpected costs.
questions.memo: Emergency funds cover surprise expenses.

questions.question: Setting money aside for later instead of spending it is called ____.
questions.memo: Saving keeps money for the future.

questions.question: Money saved for unexpected costs is an ____ fund.
questions.memo: An emergency fund is for surprises.

questions.question: To save, you should spend ____ than you earn.
questions.memo: Spending less than you earn leaves money to save.

questions.question: Saving towards a bicycle is saving with a clear ____.
questions.memo: Saving for a specific goal gives it a purpose.

questions.question: Sort each into 'Helps you save' or 'Stops you saving'.
questions.expected: Putting money aside and setting goals help you save; overspending stops you.
questions.memo: Saving habits set money aside and plan goals; overspending leaves nothing to save.

questions.question: Put the steps of saving for a goal in order.

items.text: Decide what you are saving for
Work out how much you need
Reach your goal and buy the item

questions.memo: Choose the goal, work out the cost, save regularly, then reach the goal.

EMS.G7.F4.A2.title: Banks and their services
EMS.G7.F4.A2.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G7 T4) — Savings: Banks and their services.
EMS.G7.F4.A2.recovery_strategy: Banks keep money safe, lend it out, and help with payments.

questions.question: What is one main job of a bank?
options: To give money away for free
questions.memo: Banks keep money safe and allow people to save and make payments.

questions.question: What is 'interest' that a bank pays on savings?
options: Extra money the bank pays you for saving
A fee you pay the bank
questions.expected: Extra money the bank pays you for saving
questions.memo: Interest is the reward the bank pays you for keeping savings with them.

questions.question: Which is a service banks provide?
questions.memo: Banks help people pay, save and borrow — not sell groceries or cut hair.

questions.question: Why might you keep savings in a bank instead of at home?
options: It is safer and can earn interest
questions.expected: It is safer and can earn interest
questions.memo: A bank is safer than home and may pay interest on your savings.

questions.question: A bank can lend money to customers. This service is called giving a ____.
questions.memo: When a bank lends money that must be repaid, it gives a loan.

questions.question: Using a bank card to pay in shops is an example of a bank's ____ service.
questions.memo: Cards and electronic payments are part of a bank's payment services.

questions.question: Which of these does a bank NOT usually do?
questions.memo: Selling vegetables is not a bank service; the others are.

questions.question: Interest paid by a bank is good for savers because it ____.
questions.memo: Interest adds to savings, helping them grow over time.

questions.question: When a bank lends you money, you usually pay back the loan plus ____.
questions.memo: Borrowers repay the loan plus interest — the cost of borrowing.

questions.question: Which statement about banks is correct?
options: Banks keep money safe, pay interest on savings and offer loans
questions.expected: Banks keep money safe, pay interest on savings and offer loans
questions.memo: Banks store money, pay interest and provide loans and payment services.

questions.question: Banks keep people's money safe.
questions.memo: Keeping money safe is a core banking service.

questions.question: Banks pay interest to people who save with them.
questions.memo: Savers usually earn interest on money kept in the bank.

questions.question: Banks give money to everyone for free.
questions.memo: Banks lend money that must be repaid, usually with interest — not free gifts.

questions.question: Making payments and offering loans are bank services.
questions.memo: Payments and loans are common services banks provide.

questions.question: Extra money the bank pays you for saving is called ____.
questions.memo: Interest is the bank's reward for your savings.

questions.question: Money a bank lends that must be repaid is a ____.
questions.memo: A loan is borrowed money that must be repaid.

questions.question: Keeping your money in a bank is ____ than keeping it at home.
questions.memo: Banks are safer than keeping cash at home.

questions.question: Helping customers pay for things with cards is a bank ____ service.
questions.memo: Card and electronic payments are bank payment services.

questions.question: Sort each item into 'Bank service' or 'Not a bank service'.
questions.expected: Keeping savings and giving loans are bank services; selling vegetables and cutting hair are not.
questions.memo: Banks save, lend and help with payments; they don't sell groceries or cut hair.

questions.question: Put the steps of earning interest on savings in order.

items.text: You deposit money into a savings account
The bank keeps your money safe
The bank adds interest over time
Your savings grow to a larger amount

questions.memo: Deposit, the bank safeguards it, interest is added, and savings grow.

EMS.G7.F4.A3.title: Opening accounts and savings schemes
EMS.G7.F4.A3.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G7 T4) — Savings: Opening accounts and savings schemes.
EMS.G7.F4.A3.recovery_strategy: From bank accounts to stokvels — many ways to save together.

questions.question: What is a savings account?
options: A bank account used to keep and grow savings
questions.expected: A bank account used to keep and grow savings
questions.memo: A savings account holds your savings safely and usually earns interest.

questions.question: What is a stokvel?
options: A community savings group where members contribute regularly
questions.expected: A community savings group where members contribute regularly
questions.memo: A stokvel is a community savings scheme where members pool money regularly.

questions.question: Which is usually needed to open a bank account?
questions.memo: Banks usually require ID to open an account.

questions.question: A benefit of a stokvel is that ____.
options: members save together and support each other
questions.expected: members save together and support each other
questions.memo: Stokvels help members save collectively and support one another.

questions.question: Which is a formal financial institution?
questions.memo: A bank is a formal financial institution; the others are not.

questions.question: Why might someone join a community savings scheme?
options: To save with others towards shared goals
questions.expected: To save with others towards shared goals
questions.memo: Community schemes help people save together, often for shared or seasonal needs.

questions.question: Opening a savings account allows you to ____.
options: keep money safe and earn interest
questions.expected: keep money safe and earn interest
questions.memo: A savings account safeguards money and usually earns interest.

questions.question: Which is a difference between a bank and a stokvel?
options: A bank is a formal institution; a stokvel is a community group
A stokvel is a government department
questions.expected: A bank is a formal institution; a stokvel is a community group
questions.memo: Banks are formal institutions; stokvels are informal community savings groups.

questions.question: Saving through both a bank and a stokvel shows that ____.
options: there are many ways to save
questions.expected: there are many ways to save
questions.memo: People can save in many ways — banks, stokvels and other schemes.

questions.question: A group of neighbours each pay R200 a month into a shared fund and take turns receiving the total. This is a ____.
questions.memo: Members contributing and taking turns to receive the pool is a classic stokvel.

questions.question: A savings account helps keep money safe and can earn interest.
questions.memo: Savings accounts safeguard money and usually pay interest.

questions.question: A stokvel is a community savings scheme.
questions.memo: A stokvel is a group savings arrangement in the community.

questions.question: You usually need identification to open a bank account.
questions.memo: Banks generally require ID documents to open an account.

questions.question: There is only one possible way to save money.
questions.memo: There are many ways to save — banks, stokvels and other schemes.

questions.question: A bank account used to keep and grow savings is a ____ account.
questions.memo: A savings account holds and grows your savings.

questions.question: A community savings group is called a ____.
questions.memo: A stokvel is a community savings scheme.

questions.question: To open a bank account you usually need ____ documents.
questions.memo: ID documents are normally needed to open an account.

questions.question: A bank is a formal financial ____.
questions.memo: Banks are formal financial institutions.

questions.question: Sort each into 'Formal (bank/institution)' or 'Community scheme'.

items.text: A savings account at a bank

questions.expected: Banks and bank accounts are formal; stokvels and burial societies are community schemes.
questions.memo: Banks are formal institutions; stokvels and burial societies are community savings schemes.

questions.question: Put the steps of opening and using a savings account in order.

items.text: Take your ID to the bank
Earn interest and watch your savings grow

questions.memo: Bring ID, open the account, deposit regularly, and earn interest as savings grow.

EMS.G7.B1.A1.title: Formal and informal businesses
EMS.G7.B1.A1.description: Entrepreneurship (CAPS G7 T1) — Businesses: Formal and informal businesses.
EMS.G7.B1.A1.recovery_strategy: Formal = registered and taxed; informal = small and unregistered.

questions.question: What is a formal business?
options: A registered business that pays tax and follows rules
A business that breaks the law
questions.expected: A registered business that pays tax and follows rules
questions.memo: A formal business is registered with the authorities, pays tax and follows regulations.

questions.question: What is an informal business?
questions.memo: Informal businesses are usually small and not formally registered, like a street vendor.

questions.question: Which is an example of an informal business?
questions.memo: A street vendor is typically informal and unregistered.

questions.question: Which is an advantage of a formal business?
options: It can access bank loans more easily
questions.expected: It can access bank loans more easily
questions.memo: Formal businesses, being registered, can more easily get loans and contracts.

questions.question: Which is an advantage of an informal business?
options: It is easy and cheap to start
It always pays the most tax
It must be a big company
questions.expected: It is easy and cheap to start
questions.memo: Informal businesses are quick and cheap to start with little paperwork.

questions.question: Which is a disadvantage of an informal business?
options: It often cannot get bank loans easily
questions.expected: It often cannot get bank loans easily
questions.memo: Because they are unregistered, informal businesses struggle to access loans.

questions.question: A spaza shop that is not registered is an example of a(n) ____ business.
questions.memo: An unregistered spaza shop is an informal business.

questions.question: Which of these would most likely be a formal business?
questions.memo: A registered factory is a formal business; the others are informal.

questions.question: A disadvantage of a formal business is that ____.
options: it has more paperwork and must pay tax
questions.expected: it has more paperwork and must pay tax
questions.memo: Formal businesses face more rules, paperwork and tax obligations.

questions.question: Why does the government prefer businesses to become formal?
options: They pay tax and follow consumer-protection rules
questions.expected: They pay tax and follow consumer-protection rules
questions.memo: Formal businesses pay tax and follow rules that protect workers and customers.

questions.question: A formal business is registered and pays tax.
questions.memo: Formal businesses are registered and meet tax and legal requirements.

questions.question: An informal business is usually large and listed on the stock exchange.
questions.memo: Informal businesses are usually small and unregistered, not large listed companies.

questions.question: Informal businesses are usually quick and cheap to start.
questions.memo: With little paperwork, informal businesses are easy and cheap to start.

questions.question: Formal businesses can usually access bank loans more easily than informal ones.
questions.memo: Being registered helps formal businesses qualify for loans.

questions.question: A registered business that pays tax is a ____ business.
questions.memo: Formal businesses are registered and pay tax.

questions.question: A small, unregistered business is an ____ business.
questions.memo: Informal businesses are small and usually unregistered.

questions.question: A street vendor is usually part of the ____ sector of the economy.
questions.memo: Street vendors are typical of the informal sector.

questions.question: Formal businesses must follow rules and pay ____.
questions.memo: Formal businesses pay tax and follow regulations.

questions.question: Sort each business into 'Formal' or 'Informal'.
questions.expected: Registered shops and licensed restaurants are formal; pavement sellers and unregistered barbers are informal.
questions.memo: Formal = registered, taxed, regulated; informal = small and unregistered.

questions.question: Put the steps of making a business formal in order.

items.text: An informal trader decides to grow
They keep records and pay tax
They can now access loans and bigger contracts

questions.memo: Becoming formal: decide to grow, register, keep records and pay tax, then access loans and contracts.

EMS.G7.B1.A2.title: Types of businesses
EMS.G7.B1.A2.description: Entrepreneurship (CAPS G7 T1) — Businesses: Types of businesses.
EMS.G7.B1.A2.recovery_strategy: Trading sells goods, manufacturing makes them, service does jobs.

questions.question: What does a trading business do?
questions.memo: A trading business buys finished goods and sells them to customers.

questions.question: What does a manufacturing business do?
questions.memo: A manufacturing business turns raw materials into finished products.

questions.question: What does a service business do?
questions.memo: A service business provides services, like repairs, transport or hairdressing.

questions.question: A bakery that bakes and sells its own bread is mainly a ____ business.
questions.memo: Baking bread from ingredients is manufacturing (making goods).

questions.question: A shop that buys clothes from a factory and sells them is a ____ business.
questions.memo: Buying finished clothes to resell is trading.

questions.question: A hair salon is an example of a ____ business.
questions.memo: A salon provides a service (haircuts), so it is a service business.

questions.question: Which type of business changes raw materials into new products?
questions.memo: Manufacturing transforms raw materials into finished goods.

questions.question: A taxi company that transports passengers is a ____ business.
questions.memo: Transport is a service, so a taxi company is a service business.

questions.question: Which business buys finished goods to resell at a higher price?
questions.memo: Trading businesses buy goods and resell them to make a profit.

questions.question: A furniture factory that makes tables and a shop that resells them show ____.
questions.memo: The factory manufactures; the shop trades the finished tables.

questions.question: A trading business buys and resells goods.
questions.memo: Trading businesses buy goods and sell them on.

questions.question: A manufacturing business provides only services, never goods.
questions.memo: Manufacturers make goods; service businesses provide services.

questions.question: A service business provides actions or tasks rather than physical goods.
questions.memo: Service businesses sell useful actions, like repairs or transport.

questions.question: Both formal and informal businesses can be trading, manufacturing or service businesses.
questions.memo: All three types exist in both the formal and informal sectors.

questions.question: A business that buys and resells goods is a ____ business.
questions.memo: Trading businesses buy and resell goods.

questions.question: A business that makes goods from raw materials is a ____ business.
questions.memo: Manufacturing businesses make goods.

questions.question: A business that provides haircuts or repairs is a ____ business.
questions.memo: Service businesses provide useful actions.

questions.question: A factory turning wood into chairs is doing ____.
questions.memo: Turning raw materials into products is manufacturing.

questions.question: Sort each business into 'Trading', 'Manufacturing' or 'Service'.
questions.expected: Reselling jeans is trading; baking and shoe-making are manufacturing; plumbing is a service.
questions.memo: Trading resells goods; manufacturing makes goods; service provides actions.

questions.question: Put the journey of a loaf of bread through business types in order.

items.text: A bakery manufactures bread from flour
A delivery service brings it to a customer

questions.memo: Raw material → manufacturing → trading → service brings it to the buyer.

EMS.G7.B1.A3.title: Businesses, disasters and epidemics
EMS.G7.B1.A3.description: Entrepreneurship (CAPS G7 T1) — Businesses: Businesses, disasters and epidemics.
EMS.G7.B1.A3.recovery_strategy: Businesses both make and buy — and shocks hit both sides.

questions.question: How can a business act as a producer?
options: By making or supplying goods and services
questions.expected: By making or supplying goods and services
questions.memo: Businesses produce by making or supplying goods and services for customers.

questions.question: How can a business also act as a consumer?
options: By buying supplies and resources it needs
questions.expected: By buying supplies and resources it needs
questions.memo: Businesses consume too — they buy materials, electricity and services.

questions.question: How might a natural disaster, like a flood, affect a business?
options: It can damage stock and stop trading
questions.expected: It can damage stock and stop trading
questions.memo: Disasters can destroy stock and premises and halt trading, causing losses.

questions.question: How might a health epidemic affect a business?
options: Fewer customers and staff may be able to work
questions.expected: Fewer customers and staff may be able to work
questions.memo: An epidemic can reduce customers and keep staff at home, hurting business.

questions.question: Why are businesses important as producers in a community?
options: They supply goods and services people need
questions.expected: They supply goods and services people need
questions.memo: As producers, businesses provide the goods and services a community relies on.

questions.question: A drought reduces a farm's harvest. As a producer, the farm will likely ____.
questions.memo: A drought cuts the harvest, so the farm produces and sells less.

questions.question: During an epidemic, a business buying extra cleaning supplies is acting as a ____.
questions.memo: Buying supplies makes the business a consumer of those goods.

questions.question: Which is a way a business might survive a disaster?
options: Having savings or insurance to recover
questions.expected: Having savings or insurance to recover
questions.memo: Savings and insurance help a business recover after a disaster.

questions.question: Why do disasters and epidemics affect both formal and informal businesses?
options: Both depend on customers, supplies and staff
questions.expected: Both depend on customers, supplies and staff
questions.memo: All businesses rely on customers, supplies and workers, so both types are affected.

questions.question: A business that is both producing goods and buying supplies shows that a business can be ____.
options: both a producer and a consumer
questions.expected: both a producer and a consumer
questions.memo: Businesses produce goods and consume supplies, so they are both.

questions.question: Businesses can be both producers and consumers.
questions.memo: They produce goods/services and consume supplies and resources.

questions.question: Natural disasters can damage a business's stock and premises.
questions.memo: Floods, fires and storms can destroy stock and buildings.

questions.question: A health epidemic always increases a business's profits.
questions.memo: Epidemics usually reduce customers and disrupt staff, often lowering profits.

questions.question: Both formal and informal businesses can be affected by disasters.
questions.memo: Disasters affect all businesses that rely on customers, supplies and staff.

questions.question: When a business makes or supplies goods, it acts as a ____.
questions.memo: Supplying goods makes a business a producer.

questions.question: When a business buys supplies it needs, it acts as a ____.
questions.memo: Buying supplies makes a business a consumer.

questions.question: A flood that destroys stock is an example of a natural ____.
questions.memo: Floods are natural disasters that can harm businesses.

questions.question: A widespread disease that affects many people is an ____.
questions.memo: An epidemic is a widespread outbreak of disease.

questions.question: Sort each role into 'Business as producer' or 'Business as consumer'.
questions.expected: Baking and offering services are producing; buying flour and supplies is consuming.
questions.memo: Producing = making/supplying; consuming = buying what the business needs.

questions.question: Put the effect of a flood on a small shop in order.

items.text: A flood damages the shop and its stock
The shop cannot trade for a while
The owner uses savings or insurance to recover

questions.memo: Disaster → trading stops → income is lost → savings or insurance help recovery.
