questions.question: Which best describes the relationship between government and households?
options: They exchange services, labour and taxes with each other
questions.expected: They exchange services, labour and taxes with each other
questions.memo: Government provides services and employs labour; households pay taxes and supply labour.

questions.question: Free basic water provided to poor households is an example of government as a ____.
questions.memo: Supplying free basic water is government producing a public service.

questions.question: Government provides services such as water, roads and schooling to households.
questions.memo: These are public services government produces for households.

questions.question: Government can act as a consumer by employing people from households.
questions.memo: Employing labour is a form of government consumption.

questions.question: Households pay for many government services through taxes.
questions.memo: Taxes from households help fund government services.

questions.question: Government only takes from households and never provides anything.
questions.memo: Government provides many services to households in return for taxes.

questions.question: Government acts as a ____ when it supplies services like roads and water.
questions.memo: Supplying services is government producing.

questions.question: Government acts as a ____ when it buys goods or employs workers.
questions.memo: Buying and employing is government consuming.

questions.question: Households help fund government services by paying ____.
questions.memo: Taxes are the main way households fund government.

questions.question: When a household member works as a teacher in a public school, they supply ____ to government.
questions.memo: Public-service workers supply labour to government.

questions.question: Sort each action into 'Government as producer' or 'Government as consumer' (towards households).

items.text: Employing a household member as a nurse

questions.expected: Building roads and running clinics are producing; employing and buying labour are consuming.
questions.memo: Producing = supplying services; consuming = buying goods/labour from households.

questions.question: Put the exchange between households and government in order.

items.text: Households earn income and pay taxes
Government provides services like schools and roads

questions.memo: Households pay tax, government collects it, provides services, and households use them.

EMS.G8.E1.A3.title: Government and businesses
EMS.G8.E1.A3.description: The Economy (CAPS G8 T1) — Government: Government and businesses.
EMS.G8.E1.A3.recovery_strategy: Government buys from, regulates and supports businesses.

questions.question: How can government act as a consumer towards businesses?
options: By buying goods and services from them
questions.expected: By buying goods and services from them
questions.memo: Government buys goods and services from businesses, acting as a consumer.

questions.question: How can government act as a producer towards businesses?
options: By providing services like roads and electricity they use
questions.expected: By providing services like roads and electricity they use
questions.memo: Government produces infrastructure and services businesses rely on.

questions.question: When government buys computers from a company, government is a ____.
questions.memo: Buying computers makes government a consumer of that business's goods.

questions.question: Businesses pay government ____ on their profits and sales.
questions.memo: Businesses pay taxes to government on profits and sales.

questions.question: Government building roads that businesses use to transport goods is government as a ____.
questions.memo: Providing roads is government producing a service businesses use.

questions.question: Why is good infrastructure (roads, electricity) important for businesses?
options: It helps them produce and deliver goods
questions.expected: It helps them produce and deliver goods
questions.memo: Reliable infrastructure lets businesses operate and deliver efficiently.

questions.question: Which is an example of government as a consumer of business output?
options: Buying office furniture from a supplier
questions.expected: Buying office furniture from a supplier
questions.memo: Purchasing furniture from a supplier is consuming a business's goods.

questions.question: Government can support businesses by ____.
options: providing services and a stable environment to trade
questions.expected: providing services and a stable environment to trade
questions.memo: Government supports business through infrastructure, services and stable rules.

questions.question: Which shows government as both consumer and producer for businesses?
options: It buys their goods AND provides roads they use
questions.expected: It buys their goods AND provides roads they use
questions.memo: Government consumes business goods and produces services businesses depend on.

questions.question: Taxes paid by businesses help government to ____.
questions.memo: Business taxes help fund the services government provides.

questions.question: Government can buy goods and services from businesses.
questions.memo: Government is a consumer when it purchases from businesses.

questions.question: Government provides infrastructure that businesses use.
questions.memo: Roads, electricity and other services support businesses.

questions.question: Businesses never pay any tax to government.
questions.memo: Businesses pay taxes on profits and sales.

questions.question: Government can be both a consumer of business goods and a producer of services.
questions.memo: It buys from businesses and provides services they use.

questions.question: Government acts as a ____ when it buys goods from businesses.
questions.memo: Buying from businesses is consuming.

questions.question: Government acts as a ____ when it provides roads and electricity to businesses.
questions.memo: Providing infrastructure is producing services.

questions.question: Businesses pay ____ to government on their profits.
questions.memo: Businesses pay tax on profits and sales.

questions.question: Good ____, like roads and power, helps businesses operate.
questions.memo: Infrastructure supports business activity.

questions.question: Sort each into 'Government as producer' or 'Government as consumer' (towards businesses).
questions.expected: Roads and electricity are producing; buying uniforms and computers is consuming.
questions.memo: Producing = providing services/infrastructure; consuming = buying business goods.

questions.question: Put the exchange between government and a business in order.

items.text: A business uses them to produce goods
Government buys some of the goods
The business pays tax on its profit

questions.memo: Government provides infrastructure, the business produces and sells (some to government), then pays tax.

EMS.G8.E2.A1.title: Government revenue: tax
EMS.G8.E2.A1.description: The Economy (CAPS G8 T1) — The National Budget: Government revenue: tax.
EMS.G8.E2.A1.recovery_strategy: Direct tax is on income; indirect tax is on what you buy (like VAT).

questions.question: What is government revenue?
options: The money government receives, mainly from taxes
questions.expected: The money government receives, mainly from taxes
questions.memo: Government revenue is the income government collects, largely through taxes.

questions.question: What is direct tax?
options: Tax charged directly on income or profits
Tax added to the price of goods
questions.expected: Tax charged directly on income or profits
questions.memo: Direct tax is paid directly on income or profit, like income tax.

questions.question: What is indirect tax?
options: Tax added to the price of goods and services
questions.expected: Tax added to the price of goods and services
questions.memo: Indirect tax is added to what you buy, like VAT.

questions.question: VAT (Value-Added Tax) is an example of ____.
questions.memo: VAT is added to prices of goods and services, so it is indirect tax.

questions.question: Income tax on a person's salary is an example of ____.
questions.memo: Income tax is charged directly on income, so it is direct tax.

questions.question: Why does government collect taxes?
questions.memo: Tax revenue funds public services like health, education and roads.

questions.question: Which is the main source of government revenue?
questions.memo: Taxes are the main source of government revenue.

questions.question: When you pay extra on a shop item because of VAT, you are paying ____.
questions.memo: VAT added at the till is an indirect tax.

questions.question: Which statement about direct and indirect tax is correct?
options: Direct tax is on income/profit; indirect tax is on spending
questions.expected: Direct tax is on income/profit; indirect tax is on spending
questions.memo: Direct tax targets income/profit; indirect tax targets spending on goods/services.

questions.question: More people earning and spending usually means government collects ____.
questions.memo: More income and spending generally raises tax revenue.

questions.question: Taxes are the main source of government revenue.
questions.memo: Government revenue comes mainly from taxes.

questions.question: Direct tax is charged on income or profits.
questions.memo: Direct tax targets income and profits.

questions.question: VAT is a direct tax on your salary.
questions.memo: VAT is an indirect tax added to goods and services, not a direct tax on salary.

questions.question: Tax revenue helps pay for public services.
questions.memo: Government uses tax revenue to fund public services.

questions.question: Money government receives, mostly from taxes, is government ____.
questions.memo: Government revenue is the income it collects.

questions.question: Tax charged on income or profit is ____ tax.
questions.memo: Direct tax is on income/profit.

questions.question: Tax added to the price of goods, like VAT, is ____ tax.
questions.memo: Indirect tax is added to spending.

questions.question: Government collects tax to pay for public ____.
questions.memo: Tax funds public services.

questions.question: Sort each tax into 'Direct tax' or 'Indirect tax'.

items.text: Tax added to the price of fuel

questions.expected: Income and company-profit taxes are direct; VAT and fuel tax are indirect.
questions.memo: Direct = on income/profit; indirect = added to what you buy.

questions.question: Put the flow of tax money in order.

items.text: People earn income and businesses make profit
They pay direct and indirect taxes
Government spends it on public services

questions.memo: Earn/spend → pay tax → government collects revenue → funds public services.

EMS.G8.E2.A2.title: Government expenditure
EMS.G8.E2.A2.description: The Economy (CAPS G8 T1) — The National Budget: Government expenditure.
EMS.G8.E2.A2.recovery_strategy: Tax money is spent on public services everyone uses.

questions.question: What is government expenditure?
options: The money government spends on services and projects
questions.expected: The money government spends on services and projects
questions.memo: Government expenditure is the spending government does on public services and projects.

questions.question: Which is an example of government expenditure?
questions.memo: Paying public-sector salaries is government spending.

questions.question: On which of these does government spend money?
questions.memo: Government spends on public services like health, education and housing.

questions.question: A social grant paid to a person in need is part of government ____.
questions.memo: Grants are money government pays out — expenditure.

questions.question: Why does government spend on education?
options: To build skills and improve the country's future
questions.expected: To build skills and improve the country's future
questions.memo: Education spending builds skills and supports the country's development.

questions.question: Spending on roads, bridges and electricity is spending on ____.
questions.memo: Roads, bridges and power are infrastructure.

questions.question: Which is NOT usually government expenditure?
questions.memo: A private shop's stock is its own expense, not government expenditure.

questions.question: Government spending on security includes ____.
questions.memo: Security spending covers police and defence services.

questions.question: If government spends more than it collects in revenue, it has a ____.
questions.memo: Spending more than revenue produces a budget deficit.

questions.question: Why must government plan its expenditure carefully?
options: Its revenue is limited and needs must be prioritised
questions.expected: Its revenue is limited and needs must be prioritised
questions.memo: Limited revenue means government must prioritise where to spend.

questions.question: Government expenditure is the money government spends on services.
questions.memo: Expenditure is government's spending on public services and projects.

questions.question: Social grants and salaries are forms of government expenditure.
questions.memo: Both are money government pays out.

questions.question: Government spends money on health, education and security.
questions.memo: These are major areas of government expenditure.

questions.question: Government expenditure means the tax it collects.
questions.memo: Collected tax is revenue; expenditure is what government spends.

questions.question: The money government spends on services is government ____.
questions.memo: Expenditure is government spending.

questions.question: Money paid to people in need, like a child-support grant, is a social ____.
questions.memo: Social grants support people in need.

questions.question: Roads, bridges and power lines are examples of ____.
questions.memo: These are infrastructure that government funds.

questions.question: Government spends on ____ such as schools and universities.
questions.memo: Education is a major area of government spending.

questions.question: Sort each into 'Government expenditure' or 'Government revenue'.
questions.expected: Salaries and building schools are expenditure; collecting VAT and income tax is revenue.
questions.memo: Expenditure is money out; revenue is money in (tax).

questions.question: Put the steps of government spending in order.

items.text: It plans a budget of where to spend
It spends on services like health and education

questions.memo: Collect revenue, plan the budget, spend on services, and citizens benefit.

EMS.G8.E2.A3.title: The budget, growth and inequality
EMS.G8.E2.A3.description: The Economy (CAPS G8 T1) — The National Budget: The budget, growth and inequality.
EMS.G8.E2.A3.recovery_strategy: The budget is a tool to grow the economy and reduce unfairness.

questions.question: What is the National Budget?
options: Government's plan for its revenue and spending for the year
questions.expected: Government's plan for its revenue and spending for the year
questions.memo: The National Budget plans the country's government revenue and expenditure for the year.

questions.question: How can the National Budget help economic growth?
options: By spending on infrastructure and services that support the economy
questions.expected: By spending on infrastructure and services that support the economy
questions.memo: Spending on roads, education and services helps the economy grow.

questions.question: How can the budget help reduce inequality?
options: By spending more on services for poorer communities
questions.expected: By spending more on services for poorer communities
questions.memo: Directing spending and grants to poorer communities helps reduce inequality.

questions.question: Social grants in the budget mainly help to ____.
options: support people with low or no income
questions.expected: support people with low or no income
questions.memo: Grants provide income support to the poor, reducing inequality.

questions.question: Who presents South Africa's National Budget?
questions.memo: The Minister of Finance presents the National Budget.

questions.question: Spending on education and skills in the budget can ____ over time.
questions.memo: Education spending builds skills, supporting growth and reducing inequality.

questions.question: A budget that invests in infrastructure can help businesses by ____.
options: making it easier to produce and transport goods
questions.expected: making it easier to produce and transport goods
questions.memo: Infrastructure spending supports business activity and growth.

questions.question: Why does the budget have to make choices?
options: Government revenue is limited, so it cannot fund everything fully
questions.expected: Government revenue is limited, so it cannot fund everything fully
questions.memo: Limited revenue forces the budget to prioritise spending.

questions.question: Which best shows the budget reducing inequality AND supporting growth?
options: Funding schools and clinics in poor areas while building roads
questions.expected: Funding schools and clinics in poor areas while building roads
questions.memo: Targeted services reduce inequality, while infrastructure supports growth.

questions.question: The National Budget is best described as a tool to ____.
options: plan spending to grow the economy and address inequality
questions.expected: plan spending to grow the economy and address inequality
questions.memo: The budget plans revenue and spending to grow the economy and tackle inequality.

questions.question: The National Budget is government's plan for revenue and spending.
questions.memo: It plans the year's government income and expenditure.

questions.question: Spending on infrastructure can support economic growth.
questions.memo: Infrastructure helps the economy produce and grow.

questions.question: The budget can be used to help reduce inequality.
questions.memo: Targeted spending and grants help reduce inequality.

questions.question: The National Budget only lists income and ignores spending.
questions.memo: The budget plans both revenue and expenditure.

questions.question: Government's yearly plan for revenue and spending is the National ____.
questions.memo: The National Budget plans government finances for the year.

questions.question: Spending on roads and power, called ____, can support growth.
questions.memo: Infrastructure spending supports economic growth.

questions.question: Social ____ in the budget support people with low income.
questions.memo: Grants give income support to the poor.

questions.question: The budget can help redress economic ____ by spending on poorer communities.
questions.memo: Targeted spending helps reduce inequality.

questions.question: Sort each budget choice by its main aim.
questions.expected: Roads, ports and electricity support growth; grants and clinics in poor areas reduce inequality.
questions.memo: Infrastructure tends to drive growth; targeted social spending reduces inequality.

questions.question: Put the National Budget process in order.

items.text: It plans expenditure on services and projects
The Minister of Finance presents the budget
Spending supports growth and addresses inequality

questions.memo: Estimate revenue, plan spending, present the budget, then spending drives growth and fairness.

EMS.G8.E3.A1.title: Lifestyles and types of society
EMS.G8.E3.A1.description: The Economy (CAPS G8 T1) — Standard of living: Lifestyles and types of society.
EMS.G8.E3.A1.recovery_strategy: Standard of living = how comfortably people are able to live.

questions.question: What does 'standard of living' mean?
options: How comfortably people are able to live
questions.expected: How comfortably people are able to live
questions.memo: Standard of living describes how comfortably and well people are able to live.

questions.question: A self-sufficient society is one that ____.
options: produces most of what it needs itself
questions.expected: produces most of what it needs itself
questions.memo: A self-sufficient society meets most of its own needs through its own production.

questions.question: A modern society usually has ____.
questions.memo: Modern societies typically have advanced technology, services and trade.

questions.question: A rural society is mostly found in ____.
questions.memo: Rural societies are based in the countryside, often around farming.

questions.question: Which usually improves a person's standard of living?
options: Access to good services, income and education
questions.expected: Access to good services, income and education
questions.memo: Better income, services and education raise standard of living.

questions.question: Which is a sign of a higher standard of living?
options: Reliable access to clean water and electricity
questions.expected: Reliable access to clean water and electricity
questions.memo: Reliable basic services indicate a higher standard of living.

questions.question: A society that grows its own food and makes its own goods is best described as ____.
questions.memo: Producing your own food and goods is self-sufficiency.

questions.question: Why do standards of living differ between communities?
options: Differences in income, services and opportunities
questions.expected: Differences in income, services and opportunities
questions.memo: Income, services and opportunities vary, so living standards differ.

questions.question: Which lifestyle factor is part of standard of living?
options: Quality of housing and access to services
questions.expected: Quality of housing and access to services
questions.memo: Housing quality and service access are part of living standards.

questions.question: A community moving from no electricity to reliable power has likely seen its standard of living ____.
questions.memo: Gaining reliable electricity raises the standard of living.

questions.question: Standard of living describes how comfortably people are able to live.
questions.memo: It measures how well and comfortably people live.

questions.question: A self-sufficient society produces most of what it needs itself.
questions.memo: Self-sufficiency means meeting your own needs through your own production.

questions.question: Access to services like water and electricity affects standard of living.
questions.memo: Basic services are a key part of living standards.

questions.question: Every community in a country has exactly the same standard of living.
questions.memo: Living standards differ with income, services and opportunities.

questions.question: How comfortably people are able to live is their standard of ____.
questions.memo: Standard of living measures how comfortably people live.

questions.question: A society that meets most of its own needs is ____.
questions.memo: Self-sufficient societies produce most of what they need.

questions.question: A society based in the countryside is a ____ society.
questions.memo: Rural societies are countryside-based.

questions.question: Good income, education and services usually ____ standard of living.
questions.memo: These factors raise living standards.

questions.question: Sort each into 'Higher standard of living' or 'Lower standard of living'.
questions.expected: Clean water, electricity and schools point to a higher standard; no healthcare or housing points to lower.
questions.memo: Access to services, education and housing raises living standards; lack of them lowers it.

questions.question: Put societies in order from least to most reliant on trade and technology.

items.text: A self-sufficient society making its own goods
A rural society with some trade
A growing town with shops and services
A modern society with advanced technology and trade

questions.memo: From self-sufficient, to rural with trade, to a town, to a modern high-tech society.

EMS.G8.E3.A2.title: Development, environment and unemployment
EMS.G8.E3.A2.description: The Economy (CAPS G8 T1) — Standard of living: Development, environment and unemployment.
EMS.G8.E3.A2.recovery_strategy: Higher living standards must be weighed against the environmental cost.

questions.question: How can development sometimes harm the environment?
options: Through pollution and using up natural resources
By cleaning all air for free
questions.expected: Through pollution and using up natural resources
questions.memo: Development can cause pollution and deplete resources if not managed carefully.

questions.question: What is unemployment?
options: When people who want to work cannot find jobs
questions.expected: When people who want to work cannot find jobs
questions.memo: Unemployment is when willing workers cannot find jobs.

questions.question: Why is high unemployment a problem for standard of living?
options: People without jobs earn little or no income
questions.expected: People without jobs earn little or no income
questions.memo: Without jobs, people lack income, lowering their standard of living.

questions.question: Using resources productively means ____.
options: getting good value and not wasting them
questions.expected: getting good value and not wasting them
questions.memo: Productive use gets value from resources without waste.

questions.question: Which helps promote a healthy environment?
options: Reducing pollution and using resources wisely
questions.expected: Reducing pollution and using resources wisely
questions.memo: Cutting pollution and using resources wisely protect the environment.

questions.question: Development that improves life but protects the environment is called ____.
questions.memo: Sustainable development improves lives while protecting the environment.

questions.question: Creating more jobs usually helps standard of living because ____.
questions.memo: More jobs mean more incomes, raising living standards.

questions.question: Which is an environmental cost of careless development?
questions.memo: Careless development can pollute air and water.

questions.question: Balancing development with protecting the environment matters because ____.
questions.memo: We must protect resources and the environment for the future.

questions.question: High unemployment combined with pollution would ____ a community's standard of living.
questions.memo: Joblessness and pollution both reduce well-being and living standards.

questions.question: Development can harm the environment if it is not managed carefully.
questions.memo: Unmanaged development can pollute and deplete resources.

questions.question: Unemployment means people who want jobs cannot find them.
questions.memo: Unemployment is willing workers without jobs.

questions.question: Creating jobs can improve people's standard of living.
questions.memo: Jobs provide income, raising living standards.

questions.question: Using resources productively means wasting as much as possible.
questions.memo: Productive use avoids waste and gets good value from resources.

questions.question: When willing workers cannot find jobs, there is ____.
questions.memo: Unemployment is the lack of jobs for those who want them.

questions.question: Development that protects the environment for the future is ____ development.
questions.memo: Sustainable development balances progress with protection.

questions.question: Pollution and using up resources are ____ costs of development.
questions.memo: These are environmental costs.

questions.question: More jobs usually ____ a community's standard of living.
questions.memo: Jobs bring income, raising living standards.

questions.question: Sort each into 'Helps standard of living / environment' or 'Harms it'.
questions.expected: Jobs and wise resource use help; pollution and unemployment harm.
questions.memo: Jobs and sustainability help; pollution and unemployment harm living standards.

questions.question: Put this chain about development and the environment in order.

items.text: Jobs are created and incomes rise
Pollution risks the environment if unmanaged
Sustainable choices protect resources for the future

questions.memo: Development brings jobs, but also pollution risk, so sustainable choices are needed.

EMS.G8.E4.A1.title: The goods and services market
EMS.G8.E4.A1.description: The Economy (CAPS G8 T2) — Markets: The goods and services market.
EMS.G8.E4.A1.recovery_strategy: In the goods market, households buy what businesses sell.

questions.question: What is a market in economics?
options: Where buyers and sellers trade goods or services
questions.expected: Where buyers and sellers trade goods or services
questions.memo: A market is anywhere buyers and sellers come together to trade.

questions.question: In the goods and services market, households usually ____.
questions.memo: In the goods market, households are the buyers of goods and services.

questions.question: In the goods and services market, businesses usually ____.
questions.memo: Businesses are the sellers in the goods and services market.

questions.question: Buying bread at a shop takes place in the ____ market.
questions.memo: Buying a finished product like bread is in the goods and services market.

questions.question: A market does NOT need to be ____.
questions.memo: Markets can be online or anywhere — they just need buyers, sellers and something to trade.

questions.question: Online shopping is an example of a ____ market.
questions.memo: Buying products online is still the goods and services market.

questions.question: In the goods and services market, money flows from ____.
questions.memo: Households pay businesses for goods and services, so money flows that way.

questions.question: Which is traded in the goods and services market?
options: A haircut and a loaf of bread
questions.expected: A haircut and a loaf of bread
questions.memo: Finished goods and services (bread, haircuts) are traded here.

questions.question: Why is the goods and services market important?
options: It is where people buy what they need and want
questions.expected: It is where people buy what they need and want
questions.memo: It is where consumers get the goods and services they need and want.

questions.question: A spaza shop selling cooldrinks to customers operates in the ____ market.
questions.memo: Selling cooldrinks (a good) is the goods and services market.

questions.question: A market is where buyers and sellers trade.
questions.memo: Markets bring buyers and sellers together to trade.

questions.question: In the goods and services market, households buy and businesses sell.
questions.memo: Households are buyers; businesses are sellers of goods and services.

questions.question: A market must always be a physical building.
questions.memo: Markets can be online or anywhere buyers and sellers meet.

questions.question: Buying a finished good like bread happens in the goods and services market.
questions.memo: Finished goods are traded in the goods and services market.

questions.question: A place where buyers and sellers trade is a ____.
questions.memo: A market is where trade happens.

questions.question: In the goods and services market, households are the ____.
questions.memo: Households buy goods and services.

questions.question: In the goods and services market, businesses are the ____.
questions.memo: Businesses sell goods and services.

questions.question: Buying a haircut happens in the ____ and services market.
questions.memo: Services like haircuts are traded in the goods and services market.

questions.question: Sort each into 'Goods and services market' or 'Not the goods and services market'.
questions.expected: Groceries and a bus ride are goods/services; hiring labour or a loan are factor/financial markets.
questions.memo: The goods and services market trades finished products and services, not labour or finance.

questions.question: Put a goods-and-services market transaction in order.

items.text: A business offers a good for sale
A household decides to buy it

questions.memo: Business offers, household chooses, pays, and receives the good.

EMS.G8.E4.A2.title: The factor market
EMS.G8.E4.A2.description: The Economy (CAPS G8 T2) — Markets: The factor market.
EMS.G8.E4.A2.recovery_strategy: In the factor market, businesses buy labour and finance.

questions.question: What is traded in the factor market?
options: Factors of production, like labour and finance
questions.expected: Factors of production, like labour and finance
questions.memo: The factor market trades factors of production, such as labour and capital/finance.

questions.question: In the labour market, households mainly ____.
questions.memo: Households supply (sell) labour; businesses buy it.

questions.question: What do workers receive for selling their labour?
questions.memo: Workers earn wages or salaries for their labour.

questions.question: The financial market is where ____ is borrowed and lent.
questions.memo: The financial market deals in money — borrowing, lending and investing.

questions.question: A business hiring a new worker is taking part in the ____ market.
questions.memo: Hiring labour happens in the labour part of the factor market.

questions.question: A business borrowing money from a bank uses the ____ market.
questions.memo: Borrowing money happens in the financial market.

questions.question: In the factor market, the flow of labour goes from ____.
questions.memo: Households supply labour to businesses in the factor market.

questions.question: Which is part of the factor market?
options: The labour market and the financial market
questions.expected: The labour market and the financial market
questions.memo: The factor market includes the labour and financial markets.

questions.question: How is the factor market different from the goods and services market?
options: It trades factors of production, not finished goods
questions.expected: It trades factors of production, not finished goods
questions.memo: The factor market trades inputs (labour, finance); the goods market trades finished products.

questions.question: Interest paid on a loan is a price in the ____ market.
questions.memo: Interest is the cost of borrowing money in the financial market.

questions.question: The factor market trades factors of production like labour and finance.
questions.memo: It deals in inputs such as labour and capital/finance.

questions.question: In the labour market, households sell their labour to businesses.
questions.memo: Households supply labour; businesses buy it.

questions.question: The financial market is where money is borrowed and lent.
questions.memo: It deals in finance — borrowing, lending and investing.

questions.question: Buying a loaf of bread happens in the factor market.
questions.memo: Bread is a finished good, traded in the goods and services market, not the factor market.

questions.question: The market for factors of production like labour and finance is the ____ market.
questions.memo: The factor market trades factors of production.

questions.question: Households sell their ____ in the labour market.
questions.memo: Households supply labour in the labour market.

EMS.G8.F1.A1.title: Sole trader, debit and credit
EMS.G8.F1.A1.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G8 T1) — Accounting concepts: Sole trader, debit and credit.
EMS.G8.F1.A1.recovery_strategy: A sole trader is one owner; debit and credit are the two sides of every entry.

questions.question: What is a sole trader?
options: A business owned and run by one person
questions.expected: A business owned and run by one person
questions.memo: A sole trader is a one-owner business — the simplest form for keeping accounts.

questions.question: In accounting, every transaction has two sides called ____.
questions.memo: Each transaction is recorded with a debit side and a credit side.

questions.question: On which side of an account is the debit traditionally placed?
questions.memo: By convention, debit entries go on the left of an account.

questions.question: On which side is the credit traditionally placed?
questions.memo: Credit entries go on the right of an account.

questions.question: Why does a sole trader keep accounting records?
options: To track the business's money and know its profit
questions.expected: To track the business's money and know its profit
questions.memo: Records let the owner track money and work out profit or loss.

questions.question: For every debit entry, there must be an equal ____.
questions.memo: Double-entry means each debit has an equal and opposite credit.

questions.question: Who is responsible for a sole trader's debts?
questions.memo: A sole trader's owner is personally responsible for the business's debts.

questions.question: The words 'debit' and 'credit' are used to ____.
options: record the two sides of each transaction
questions.expected: record the two sides of each transaction
questions.memo: Debit and credit record the two sides of every transaction.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about a sole trader?
options: It has one owner who keeps the profit and carries the risk
It pays no attention to records
questions.expected: It has one owner who keeps the profit and carries the risk
questions.memo: A sole trader's single owner keeps profit and carries the risk.

questions.question: In double-entry bookkeeping, total debits should always ____ total credits.
questions.memo: Total debits must equal total credits — that is the balance check.

questions.question: A sole trader is a business owned by one person.
questions.memo: Sole traders have a single owner.

questions.question: Every transaction has a debit side and a credit side.
questions.memo: Double-entry records each transaction with a debit and a credit.

questions.question: Debit means the right side of an account.
questions.memo: Debit is the left side; credit is the right side.

questions.question: Total debits should equal total credits.
questions.memo: Debits and credits must balance in double-entry bookkeeping.

questions.memo: A sole trader has one owner.

questions.memo: Debit and credit are the two sides.

questions.memo: Debit = left, credit = right.

questions.question: Credit is recorded on the ____ side of an account.
questions.memo: Credit entries go on the right.

questions.question: Sort each into 'Debit side' or 'Credit side' of an account.
questions.expected: Debit is the left side; credit is the right side.
questions.memo: Debit = left side; credit = right side of an account.

questions.question: Put the idea of recording a transaction in order.

items.text: It is recorded with a debit on one account
And an equal credit on another account

questions.memo: A transaction is recorded as an equal debit and credit, keeping the books balanced.

EMS.G8.F1.A2.title: The accounting equation
EMS.G8.F1.A2.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G8 T1) — Accounting concepts: The accounting equation.
EMS.G8.F1.A2.recovery_strategy: The equation always balances: what you own = your stake + what you owe.

questions.question: What is the accounting equation?
questions.memo: The accounting equation is A = OE + L.

questions.question: In A = OE + L, what does 'A' stand for?
questions.memo: A stands for Assets — what the business owns.

questions.question: In A = OE + L, what does 'OE' stand for?
questions.memo: OE is Owner's equity — the owner's stake in the business.

questions.question: In A = OE + L, what does 'L' stand for?
questions.memo: L stands for Liabilities — what the business owes.

questions.question: The accounting equation must always ____.
questions.memo: Both sides of the equation must always be equal (balance).

questions.question: If assets are R10 000 and liabilities are R4 000, owner's equity is ____.
Owner's equity is best described as ____.
options: the owner's share of the business
questions.expected: the owner's share of the business
questions.memo: Owner's equity is the owner's claim on the business's assets.

questions.question: If a business has assets of R8 000 and owner's equity of R5 000, liabilities are ____.
Why is the accounting equation useful?
options: It shows the business always balances what it owns against equity and debt
questions.expected: It shows the business always balances what it owns against equity and debt
questions.memo: It shows assets are always financed by owner's equity plus liabilities.

questions.question: Which is another correct form of the equation?
questions.memo: Rearranging A = OE + L gives OE = A − L.

questions.question: The accounting equation is Assets = Owner's equity + Liabilities.
questions.memo: A = OE + L is the accounting equation.

questions.question: Assets are what the business owns.
questions.memo: Assets are the resources the business owns.

questions.question: Liabilities are what the business owns.
questions.memo: Liabilities are what the business owes; assets are what it owns.

questions.question: The two sides of the accounting equation must always be equal.
questions.memo: The equation always balances.

questions.question: The accounting equation is Assets = Owner's equity + ____.
questions.memo: A = OE + L.

questions.question: Assets are what the business ____.
questions.memo: Assets are owned resources.

questions.question: Liabilities are what the business ____.
questions.memo: Liabilities are debts owed.

questions.question: Owner's equity = Assets ____ Liabilities.
questions.memo: OE = A − L.

questions.question: Sort each item into 'Asset', 'Liability' or 'Owner's equity'.
questions.expected: Cash and equipment are assets; a loan is a liability; the owner's capital is owner's equity.
questions.memo: Owned = asset; owed = liability; owner's stake = owner's equity.

questions.question: Put the steps of using the accounting equation in order.
questions.memo: Assets − Liabilities = Owner's equity.

EMS.G8.F1.A3.title: Effect of transactions on the equation
EMS.G8.F1.A3.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G8 T1) — Accounting concepts: Effect of transactions on the equation.
EMS.G8.F1.A3.recovery_strategy: Every transaction touches at least two parts, keeping the equation balanced.

questions.question: If the owner deposits more capital as cash, what happens?
options: Assets increase and owner's equity increases
questions.expected: Assets increase and owner's equity increases
questions.memo: More cash (asset) and a bigger owner's stake (equity) both rise — the equation stays balanced.

questions.question: Every transaction affects ____ of the accounting equation.
questions.memo: Each transaction touches at least two parts, keeping A = OE + L balanced.

questions.question: If the business buys equipment for cash, what happens to assets?
options: One asset (equipment) rises while another (cash) falls
questions.expected: One asset (equipment) rises while another (cash) falls
questions.memo: Cash falls and equipment rises — total assets stay the same.

questions.question: If the business takes a bank loan in cash, what happens?
questions.memo: Cash rises (asset up) and the loan is a new liability — both sides rise equally.

questions.question: After any transaction, the accounting equation must still ____.
questions.memo: The equation must remain balanced after every transaction.

questions.question: If the business pays off part of a loan with cash, what happens?
questions.memo: Cash falls (asset down) and the loan owed falls (liability down) — still balanced.

questions.question: Earning income (a profit) generally increases ____.
questions.memo: Profit increases owner's equity (the owner's stake in the business).

questions.question: Paying an expense in cash generally ____.
options: reduces assets and reduces owner's equity
questions.expected: reduces assets and reduces owner's equity
questions.memo: An expense reduces cash (asset) and reduces owner's equity (profit/stake).

questions.question: Why must a transaction touch at least two parts of the equation?
questions.memo: Touching two parts keeps both sides equal, so the equation stays balanced.

questions.question: If assets increase by R500 and liabilities do not change, owner's equity must ____.
questions.memo: To keep A = OE + L balanced, if assets rise R500 and liabilities are unchanged, owner's equity rises R500.

questions.question: Every transaction affects at least two parts of the accounting equation.
questions.memo: Each transaction touches two or more parts, keeping it balanced.

questions.question: Buying equipment for cash changes the make-up of assets but not their total.
questions.memo: Cash down, equipment up — total assets stay the same.

questions.question: Taking a loan in cash increases both assets and liabilities.
questions.memo: Cash rises (asset) and the loan is a new liability.

questions.question: After a transaction, the accounting equation can be left unbalanced.
questions.memo: The equation must always remain balanced after every transaction.

questions.question: Each transaction must keep the accounting equation in ____.
questions.memo: The equation stays balanced after every transaction.

questions.question: Buying equipment for cash makes equipment rise and cash ____.
questions.memo: Cash falls while equipment rises; total assets unchanged.

questions.question: Taking a loan in cash increases assets and ____.
questions.memo: The loan is a new liability while cash (asset) rises.

questions.question: Earning a profit increases the owner's ____.
questions.memo: Profit increases owner's equity.

Take a cash loan from the bank

questions.memo: Watch total assets: capital/loan in = up; expense out = down; asset-for-asset swap = unchanged.

questions.question: Put the reasoning for keeping the equation balanced in order.

items.text: Record equal changes so both sides match

questions.memo: Identify the affected parts, record equal changes, and the equation stays balanced.

EMS.G8.F2.A1.title: Receipts and deposit slips
EMS.G8.F2.A1.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G8 T1) — Source documents: Receipts and deposit slips.

questions.question: What is a source document?
options: The written proof that a transaction took place
questions.expected: The written proof that a transaction took place
questions.memo: Source documents are the paper (or digital) proof that a transaction happened.

questions.question: What is a receipt?
questions.memo: A receipt is issued as proof that money was received.

questions.question: What is a deposit slip used for?
options: Proof that money was paid into a bank account
questions.expected: Proof that money was paid into a bank account
questions.memo: A deposit slip is proof of money deposited into a bank account.

questions.question: A till slip (cash register slip) is given to ____.
options: a customer as proof of a cash sale
questions.expected: a customer as proof of a cash sale
questions.memo: A till slip proves a cash sale to the customer.

questions.question: Why are source documents important?
options: They provide evidence to record transactions accurately
questions.expected: They provide evidence to record transactions accurately
questions.memo: Source documents give the evidence used to record transactions correctly.

questions.question: When a business receives cash from a customer, it issues a ____.
questions.memo: A receipt proves money was received from the customer.

questions.question: A deposit slip would be completed when ____.
questions.memo: Deposit slips are used when banking (depositing) money.

questions.question: Which document proves money came IN to the business?
questions.memo: A receipt proves money received (in).

questions.question: Keeping source documents helps a business to ____.
options: keep accurate records and check its accounts
questions.expected: keep accurate records and check its accounts

EMS.G8.F2.A2.title: Cheques and counterfoils
EMS.G8.F2.A2.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G8 T1) — Source documents: Cheques and counterfoils.

questions.question: What is a cheque?
options: A written instruction to a bank to pay money from an account
questions.expected: A written instruction to a bank to pay money from an account
questions.memo: A cheque instructs the bank to pay a stated amount from the writer's account.

questions.question: What is a cheque counterfoil?
options: The stub kept as a record of the cheque written
questions.expected: The stub kept as a record of the cheque written
questions.memo: The counterfoil is the stub kept as a record of the cheque.

questions.question: Why keep a cheque counterfoil?
options: As a record of the payment made
questions.expected: As a record of the payment made

EMS.G8.F4.A1.title: Concept and columns of the CRJ
EMS.G8.F4.A1.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G8 T2) — Cash Receipts Journal (service): Concept and columns of the CRJ.
EMS.G8.F4.A1.recovery_strategy: The CRJ lists all the money the business receives.

questions.question: What is the Cash Receipts Journal (CRJ)?
options: A journal that records all cash received by the business
A journal of cash paid out
questions.expected: A journal that records all cash received by the business
questions.memo: The CRJ records all cash the business receives.

questions.question: Which transactions belong in the CRJ?
questions.memo: Only cash received is recorded in the CRJ.

questions.question: Why does the CRJ have columns?
options: To organise different types of money received
To make it look nice only
questions.expected: To organise different types of money received
questions.memo: Columns group different kinds of receipts for easy totalling.

questions.question: A 'bank' column in the CRJ usually shows ____.
questions.memo: The bank column totals the cash deposited/banked.

questions.question: The CRJ is used by a ____ business in Grade 8.
questions.memo: In Grade 8 the CRJ is studied for a service business.

questions.question: Recording receipts in one journal helps the business to ____.
options: see all its income in an organised way
questions.expected: see all its income in an organised way
questions.memo: The CRJ organises all receipts in one place.

questions.question: Which is an example of an entry that would appear in the CRJ?
questions.memo: Service income received in cash is a CRJ entry.

questions.question: The CRJ is part of the ____.
questions.memo: The CRJ is one of the journals in the accounting cycle.

questions.question: Columns in the CRJ are totalled so the business can ____.
options: add up each type of receipt
questions.expected: add up each type of receipt
questions.memo: Totalling columns sums each category of receipt.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about the CRJ?
options: It records cash received and uses columns to organise it
It is the same as a bank statement
questions.expected: It records cash received and uses columns to organise it
questions.memo: The CRJ records cash received, organised in columns.

questions.question: The CRJ records all cash received by the business.
questions.memo: The CRJ is for cash received.

questions.question: The CRJ records cash paid out.
questions.memo: Cash paid out goes in the Cash Payments Journal, not the CRJ.

questions.question: Columns help organise different types of receipts in the CRJ.
questions.memo: Columns group receipts by type for easy totalling.

questions.question: The CRJ is part of the accounting cycle.
questions.memo: It is one of the journals in the cycle.

questions.question: The journal that records cash received is the Cash ____ Journal.
questions.memo: The CRJ records cash received.

questions.question: The CRJ records cash coming ____.
questions.memo: The CRJ is for cash in.

questions.question: Different types of receipts are organised using ____ in the CRJ.
questions.memo: Columns organise the receipts.

questions.question: In Grade 8 the CRJ is studied for a ____ business.
questions.memo: The Grade 8 CRJ is for a service business.

questions.question: Sort each into 'Belongs in the CRJ' or 'Does not belong in the CRJ'.

buckets.label: Does NOT belong in the CRJ

questions.expected: Cash received belongs in the CRJ; cash paid out belongs in the CPJ instead.
questions.memo: CRJ = cash received only; payments go in the CPJ.

questions.question: Put the idea of using the CRJ in order.

items.text: A receipt or till slip proves it
It is entered in the CRJ in the right column

questions.memo: Cash received → source document → recorded in the CRJ column → columns totalled.

EMS.G8.F4.A2.title: Entering receipts in the CRJ
EMS.G8.F4.A2.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G8 T2) — Cash Receipts Journal (service): Entering receipts in the CRJ.
EMS.G8.F4.A2.recovery_strategy: Each receipt becomes one line in the CRJ.

EMS.G8.F4.A3.title: Closing off the CRJ
EMS.G8.F4.A3.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G8 T2) — Cash Receipts Journal (service): Closing off the CRJ.
EMS.G8.F4.A3.recovery_strategy: Totalling the CRJ feeds the ledger and keeps the equation balanced.

EMS.G8.F5.A1.title: Concept and columns of the CPJ
EMS.G8.F5.A1.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G8 T3) — Cash Payments Journal (service): Concept and columns of the CPJ.
EMS.G8.F5.A1.recovery_strategy: The CPJ lists all the money the business pays out.

questions.question: What is the Cash Payments Journal (CPJ)?
options: A journal that records all cash paid out by the business
questions.expected: A journal that records all cash paid out by the business
questions.memo: The CPJ records all cash the business pays out.

questions.question: Which transactions belong in the CPJ?
questions.memo: Only cash paid out is recorded in the CPJ.

questions.question: Why does the CPJ have columns?
options: To organise different types of payments
questions.expected: To organise different types of payments
questions.memo: Columns group different kinds of payments for easy totalling.

questions.question: Which is an example of a CPJ entry?
questions.memo: Paying rent (cash out) is a CPJ entry.

questions.question: The CPJ is used by a ____ business in Grade 8.
questions.memo: In Grade 8 the CPJ is studied for a service business.

questions.question: Recording payments in one journal helps the business to ____.
options: see all its spending in an organised way
questions.expected: see all its spending in an organised way
questions.memo: The CPJ organises all payments in one place.

questions.question: Which column might a CPJ have?
options: A 'bank' column for total cash paid
questions.expected: A 'bank' column for total cash paid
questions.memo: The bank column totals the cash paid out.

questions.question: The CPJ is part of the ____.
questions.memo: The CPJ is one of the journals in the accounting cycle.

questions.question: The CRJ and CPJ together record ____.
options: all the cash in and out of the business
questions.expected: all the cash in and out of the business
questions.memo: CRJ (in) and CPJ (out) together capture all cash flows.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about the CPJ?
options: It records cash paid out and uses columns to organise it
It is the same as a receipt
questions.expected: It records cash paid out and uses columns to organise it
questions.memo: The CPJ records cash paid out, organised in columns.

questions.question: The CPJ records all cash paid out by the business.
questions.memo: The CPJ is for cash paid out.

questions.question: The CPJ records cash received.
questions.memo: Cash received goes in the CRJ, not the CPJ.

questions.question: Columns help organise different types of payments in the CPJ.
questions.memo: Columns group payments by type.

questions.question: The CRJ and CPJ together capture all the cash in and out.
questions.memo: Together they record all cash flows.

questions.question: The journal that records cash paid out is the Cash ____ Journal.
questions.memo: The CPJ records cash paid out.

questions.question: The CPJ records cash going ____.
questions.memo: The CPJ is for cash out.

questions.question: Different types of payments are organised using ____ in the CPJ.
questions.memo: Columns organise the payments.

questions.question: The CRJ records cash in; the CPJ records cash ____.
questions.memo: CRJ = in, CPJ = out.

questions.question: Sort each into 'Belongs in the CPJ' or 'Belongs in the CRJ'.
questions.expected: Payments (rent, wages) belong in the CPJ; receipts belong in the CRJ.
questions.memo: CPJ = cash out; CRJ = cash in.

questions.question: Put the idea of using the CPJ in order.

items.text: A cheque counterfoil or receipt proves it
It is entered in the CPJ in the right column

questions.memo: Cash paid → source document → recorded in the CPJ column → columns totalled.

EMS.G8.F5.A2.title: Entering and closing the CPJ
EMS.G8.F5.A2.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G8 T3) — Cash Payments Journal (service): Entering and closing the CPJ.
EMS.G8.F5.A2.recovery_strategy: Each payment becomes one line in the CPJ.

EMS.G8.F5.A3.title: Combined CRJ and CPJ
EMS.G8.F5.A3.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G8 T3) — Cash Payments Journal (service): Combined CRJ and CPJ.
EMS.G8.F5.A3.recovery_strategy: Together the two journals capture all the business's cash.

EMS.G8.F6.A1.title: Double-entry and T-accounts
EMS.G8.F6.A1.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G8 T4) — General Ledger and Trial Balance (service): Double-entry and T-accounts.
EMS.G8.F6.A1.recovery_strategy: Every entry has a debit side and a credit side — that's double entry.

questions.question: What is the double-entry principle?
options: Every transaction is recorded with an equal debit and credit
questions.expected: Every transaction is recorded with an equal debit and credit
questions.memo: Double-entry records each transaction twice — a debit and an equal credit.

questions.question: Why is it called 'double' entry?
options: Each transaction has two sides: debit and credit
It is written in two books only
It is done twice a year
questions.expected: Each transaction has two sides: debit and credit
questions.memo: Two sides — a debit and a credit — give double-entry its name.

questions.question: What is a 'T-account'?
options: A way of drawing an account with a debit and credit side
questions.expected: A way of drawing an account with a debit and credit side
questions.memo: A T-account is the T-shaped layout showing debit (left) and credit (right) sides.

questions.question: In a T-account, the debit side is on the ____.
questions.memo: Debit is the left side of the T-account.

questions.question: In a T-account, the credit side is on the ____.
questions.memo: Credit is the right side of the T-account.

questions.question: The General Ledger is ____.
options: the book containing all the accounts
questions.expected: the book containing all the accounts
questions.memo: The General Ledger holds all the business's accounts.

questions.question: Under double-entry, total debits must ____ total credits.
questions.memo: Debits must equal credits — the books stay balanced.

questions.question: Why use double-entry?
options: It keeps the books balanced and helps catch errors
questions.expected: It keeps the books balanced and helps catch errors
questions.memo: Double-entry keeps the equation balanced and helps detect mistakes.

questions.question: Each account in the General Ledger can be drawn as a ____.
questions.memo: Ledger accounts are often drawn as T-accounts.

questions.question: Which statement is correct?
options: Double-entry records a debit and an equal credit for each transaction
questions.expected: Double-entry records a debit and an equal credit for each transaction
questions.memo: Each transaction has an equal debit and credit under double-entry.

questions.question: Double-entry records each transaction with a debit and an equal credit.
questions.memo: Every transaction has two equal sides.

questions.question: A T-account has a debit side and a credit side.
questions.memo: The T-account shows debit (left) and credit (right).

questions.question: In a T-account, the credit side is on the left.
questions.memo: Credit is on the right; debit is on the left.

questions.question: The General Ledger contains all the business's accounts.
questions.memo: The General Ledger holds all the accounts.

questions.question: Recording each transaction with an equal debit and credit is the ____-entry principle.
questions.memo: It is the double-entry principle.

questions.question: An account drawn with a debit and credit side is a ____-account.
questions.memo: A T-account shows the two sides.

questions.question: The book that contains all the accounts is the General ____.
questions.memo: The General Ledger holds all accounts.

questions.question: Under double-entry, total debits must ____ total credits.
questions.memo: Debits equal credits.

questions.question: Sort each into 'Debit side' or 'Credit side' of a T-account.
questions.expected: Debit is the left side; credit is the right side of the T-account.
questions.memo: T-account: debit = left, credit = right.

questions.question: Put the idea of double-entry in order.

items.text: Another account is credited by the same amount

questions.memo: Debit one account, credit another by the same amount, and debits equal credits.

EMS.G8.F6.A2.title: Posting to the General Ledger
EMS.G8.F6.A2.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G8 T4) — General Ledger and Trial Balance (service): Posting to the General Ledger.
EMS.G8.F6.A2.recovery_strategy: Posting copies the journal totals into the ledger accounts.

EMS.G8.F6.A3.title: Balancing and the Trial Balance
EMS.G8.F6.A3.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G8 T4) — General Ledger and Trial Balance (service): Balancing and the Trial Balance.
EMS.G8.F6.A3.recovery_strategy: A Trial Balance checks that total debits equal total credits.

EMS.G8.B1.A1.title: Capital
EMS.G8.B1.A1.description: Entrepreneurship (CAPS G8 T2) — Factors of production: Capital.
EMS.G8.B1.A1.recovery_strategy: Capital is the money and equipment a business uses to operate.

questions.question: What is 'capital' as a factor of production?
options: The money and equipment used to run a business
questions.expected: The money and equipment used to run a business
questions.memo: Capital is the money, tools and equipment used to produce goods and services.

questions.question: What is 'own capital'?
options: Money the owner puts into the business
questions.expected: Money the owner puts into the business
questions.memo: Own capital is the owner's own money invested in the business.

questions.question: What is 'borrowed capital'?
options: Money borrowed, such as a bank loan
questions.expected: Money borrowed, such as a bank loan
questions.memo: Borrowed capital is money the business borrows and must repay.

questions.question: Which is an example of capital in a bakery?
questions.memo: Equipment like ovens and mixers is capital.

questions.question: Borrowed capital usually must be repaid with ____.
questions.memo: Borrowed capital (like a loan) is repaid with interest.

questions.question: Why does a business need capital?
options: To buy equipment and run operations
questions.expected: To buy equipment and run operations
questions.memo: Capital funds the equipment and running of the business.

questions.question: An owner using R30 000 of savings to buy stock is using ____.
questions.memo: The owner's own savings invested are own capital.

questions.question: A R50 000 bank loan to buy a delivery van is ____.
questions.memo: A bank loan is borrowed capital.

questions.question: Which is a risk of using too much borrowed capital?
options: The business must repay it with interest, even in hard times
It never has to be repaid
questions.expected: The business must repay it with interest, even in hard times
questions.memo: Borrowed capital must be repaid with interest, which is risky if income drops.

questions.question: Capital as a factor of production is rewarded with ____.
questions.memo: Capital earns interest as its reward (factor payment).

questions.question: Capital includes the money and equipment used in a business.
questions.memo: Capital is the money, tools and equipment used to produce.

questions.question: Own capital is money the owner contributes; borrowed capital is a loan.
questions.memo: Own capital is the owner's; borrowed capital is borrowed and repaid.

questions.question: Borrowed capital never has to be repaid.
questions.memo: Borrowed capital must be repaid, usually with interest.

questions.question: Machines and equipment are examples of capital.
questions.memo: Equipment used to produce is capital.

questions.question: Money and equipment used to run a business is the factor called ____.
questions.memo: Capital is money and equipment used in production.

questions.question: The owner's own money invested in the business is ____ capital.
questions.memo: Own capital is the owner's contribution.

questions.question: A bank loan used in a business is ____ capital.
questions.memo: Borrowed capital is borrowed money like a loan.

questions.question: Capital is rewarded with ____.
questions.memo: Interest is the reward to capital.

questions.question: Sort each into 'Own capital' or 'Borrowed capital'.

items.text: The owner's personal savings put in
Money the owner inherited and invested
Credit from a supplier that must be repaid

questions.expected: The owner's own savings and inheritance are own capital; loans and supplier credit are borrowed.
questions.memo: Own capital comes from the owner; borrowed capital is borrowed and repaid with interest.

questions.question: Put the steps of using capital to start a business in order.

items.text: Use the capital to produce and earn income

questions.memo: Use own capital, add borrowed capital if needed, buy equipment, then produce.

EMS.G8.B1.A2.title: Labour
EMS.G8.B1.A2.description: Entrepreneurship (CAPS G8 T2) — Factors of production: Labour.
EMS.G8.B1.A2.recovery_strategy: Labour is the human effort; skill levels differ and so does pay.

questions.question: What is 'labour' as a factor of production?
options: The human effort and work used to produce
questions.expected: The human effort and work used to produce
questions.memo: Labour is the human effort, physical and mental, used in production.

questions.question: What is unskilled labour?
questions.memo: Unskilled labour requires little training, like basic manual tasks.

questions.question: What is skilled labour?
options: Work needing training, qualifications or expertise
questions.expected: Work needing training, qualifications or expertise
questions.memo: Skilled labour needs training or expertise, like an electrician or accountant.

questions.question: Semi-skilled labour falls ____ unskilled and skilled labour.
questions.memo: Semi-skilled labour needs some training, between unskilled and fully skilled.

questions.question: Labour as a factor of production is rewarded with ____.
questions.memo: Labour earns wages or salaries as its reward.

questions.question: What are 'fair employment practices'?
options: Treating workers fairly and within the law
questions.expected: Treating workers fairly and within the law
questions.memo: Fair employment practices mean treating workers justly and legally.

questions.question: A qualified doctor is an example of ____ labour.
questions.memo: A doctor's training makes this skilled labour.

questions.question: A worker carrying boxes with no special training is doing ____ labour.
questions.memo: Basic manual work with little training is unskilled labour.

questions.question: Why are fair employment practices important?
options: They protect workers' rights and dignity
questions.expected: They protect workers' rights and dignity
questions.memo: Fair practices protect workers and create a better workplace.

questions.question: Which order shows labour from least to most training?
questions.memo: Training increases from unskilled to semi-skilled to skilled.

questions.question: Labour is the human effort used in production.
questions.memo: Labour is the human work used to produce goods and services.

questions.question: Skilled labour needs training or qualifications.
questions.memo: Skilled labour requires training or expertise.

questions.question: Labour is rewarded with interest.
questions.memo: Labour is rewarded with wages or salaries; interest is the reward to capital.

questions.question: Fair employment practices treat workers justly and lawfully.
questions.memo: Fair practices respect workers' rights and the law.

questions.question: The human effort used to produce is the factor called ____.
questions.memo: Labour is human effort in production.

questions.question: Work needing little training is ____ labour.
questions.memo: Unskilled labour needs little training.

questions.question: Work needing qualifications or expertise is ____ labour.
questions.memo: Skilled labour needs training or expertise.

questions.question: Labour is rewarded with ____.
questions.memo: Wages or salaries reward labour.

questions.question: Sort each job into 'Unskilled', 'Semi-skilled' or 'Skilled' labour.

items.text: Operating a till after short training

questions.expected: Sweeping and carrying boxes are unskilled; a trained cashier is semi-skilled; an electrician is skilled.
questions.memo: More training = more skilled: unskilled → semi-skilled → skilled.

questions.question: Put labour types in order from least to most training needed.
questions.memo: Training rises from unskilled to semi-skilled to skilled to specialised expert.

EMS.G8.B1.A3.title: Natural resources and entrepreneurship
EMS.G8.B1.A3.description: Entrepreneurship (CAPS G8 T2) — Factors of production: Natural resources and entrepreneurship.
EMS.G8.B1.A3.recovery_strategy: Four factors: land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship — each earns a reward.

questions.question: What are 'natural resources' as a factor of production?
options: Things from nature used to produce, like land, water and minerals
questions.expected: Things from nature used to produce, like land, water and minerals
questions.memo: Natural resources are gifts of nature — land, water, minerals — used in production.

questions.question: Natural resources (land) are rewarded with ____.
questions.memo: Land/natural resources earn rent as their factor reward.

questions.question: What does the entrepreneur contribute as a factor of production?
options: The idea, risk-taking and organising of the other factors
questions.expected: The idea, risk-taking and organising of the other factors
questions.memo: The entrepreneur supplies the idea, takes the risk and combines the other factors.

questions.question: The entrepreneur is rewarded with ____.
questions.memo: The entrepreneur's reward is profit.

questions.question: Which is a natural resource?
options: Water used by a bottling plant
questions.expected: Water used by a bottling plant
questions.memo: Water from nature is a natural resource; the others are capital or labour.

questions.question: How many factors of production are there in total?
questions.memo: The four factors are land (natural resources), labour, capital and entrepreneurship.

questions.question: The factor that combines and organises all the others is ____.
questions.memo: The entrepreneur brings together land, labour and capital.

questions.question: Minerals mined from the ground are an example of ____.
questions.memo: Minerals are natural resources.

questions.question: Why must natural resources be used sustainably?
options: Many cannot be replaced once used up
questions.expected: Many cannot be replaced once used up
questions.memo: Many natural resources are limited or non-renewable, so they must be used sustainably.

questions.question: Which correctly matches a factor to its reward?
questions.memo: Each factor has its own reward: wages, interest, rent and profit.

questions.question: Land, water and minerals are natural resources.
questions.memo: These come from nature and are natural resources.

questions.question: The entrepreneur takes the risk and organises the other factors.
questions.memo: The entrepreneur brings the idea, takes risk and combines the factors.

questions.question: The entrepreneur is rewarded with rent.
questions.memo: The entrepreneur earns profit; rent is the reward to land/natural resources.

questions.question: There are four factors of production.
questions.memo: Land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship are the four factors.

questions.question: Things from nature used to produce, like minerals, are ____ resources.
questions.memo: Natural resources come from nature.

questions.question: Land and natural resources are rewarded with ____.
questions.memo: Rent rewards land/natural resources.

questions.question: The person who takes the risk and combines the factors is the ____.
questions.memo: The entrepreneur organises the other factors.

questions.question: The entrepreneur is rewarded with ____.
questions.memo: Profit rewards the entrepreneur.

questions.question: Match each factor of production to its reward.
questions.expected: Labour earns wages, capital earns interest, land earns rent, entrepreneurship earns profit.
questions.memo: Wages–labour, interest–capital, rent–land, profit–entrepreneur.

questions.question: Put the factors of production together in the order an entrepreneur uses them.

items.text: The entrepreneur has a business idea
They hire labour and obtain natural resources
The factors combine to produce goods for profit

questions.memo: Idea first, then capital, then labour and resources, combining to produce for profit.

EMS.G8.B2.A1.title: Sole trader and partnership
EMS.G8.B2.A1.description: Entrepreneurship (CAPS G8 T3) — Forms of ownership: Sole trader and partnership.
EMS.G8.B2.A1.recovery_strategy: Sole trader = one owner; partnership = a few owners sharing.

questions.question: What is a sole trader?
options: A business owned by one person
questions.expected: A business owned by one person
questions.memo: A sole trader is a business owned and run by one person.

questions.question: What is a partnership?
options: A business owned by two or more people together
A business owned by one person
questions.expected: A business owned by two or more people together
questions.memo: A partnership is owned by two or more people who share it.

questions.question: An advantage of a sole trader is that ____.
options: the owner makes all decisions quickly
profits must be split many ways
it must be a big company
questions.expected: the owner makes all decisions quickly
questions.memo: A sole owner can decide quickly and keeps all the profit.

questions.question: A disadvantage of a sole trader is that ____.
options: the owner carries all the risk alone
questions.expected: the owner carries all the risk alone
questions.memo: The sole owner bears all the risk and losses alone.

questions.question: An advantage of a partnership is that ____.
options: partners share work, skills and capital
questions.expected: partners share work, skills and capital
questions.memo: Partners pool skills, work and capital.

questions.question: A disadvantage of a partnership is that ____.
options: partners may disagree and must share profits
questions.expected: partners may disagree and must share profits
questions.memo: Partners can disagree, and profits are split between them.

questions.question: A hairdresser who owns and runs her salon alone is a ____.
questions.memo: One owner running the business is a sole trader.

questions.question: Two friends who open and co-own a coffee shop form a ____.
questions.memo: Two co-owners form a partnership.

questions.question: In a sole trader, the profits ____.
options: all belong to the one owner
questions.expected: all belong to the one owner
questions.memo: A sole trader keeps all the profit (and bears all losses).

questions.question: Which statement is correct?
options: A sole trader has one owner; a partnership has two or more
A partnership has only one owner
questions.expected: A sole trader has one owner; a partnership has two or more
questions.memo: Sole trader = one owner; partnership = two or more.

questions.question: A sole trader is owned by one person.
questions.memo: Sole traders have a single owner.

questions.question: A partnership is owned by two or more people.
questions.memo: Partnerships have two or more owners.

questions.question: In a sole trader, profits are shared among many shareholders.
questions.memo: A sole trader keeps all the profit; sharing among shareholders describes a company.

questions.question: Partners can share skills and capital but may also disagree.
questions.memo: Partnerships pool resources but can have disagreements.

questions.question: A business owned by one person is a ____ trader.
questions.memo: A sole trader has one owner.

questions.question: A business owned by two or more people is a ____.
questions.memo: A partnership has two or more owners.

questions.question: A sole trader keeps ____ the profit.
questions.memo: The sole owner keeps all the profit.

questions.question: In a partnership, profits are ____ among the partners.
questions.memo: Partners share the profits.

questions.question: Sort each feature under 'Sole trader' or 'Partnership'.

items.text: Two or more owners share the work
All profit goes to a single owner
Owners pool their skills and capital

questions.expected: One owner and all-profit-to-one are sole-trader features; shared work and pooled capital are partnership features.
questions.memo: Sole trader = one owner, all profit/risk; partnership = shared ownership, work and profit.

questions.question: Put the steps of forming a partnership in order.

items.text: Two or more people agree to start a business together
They each contribute capital and skills

questions.memo: Agree to partner, contribute, run it together, then share the profits.

EMS.G8.B2.A2.title: Companies and close corporations
EMS.G8.B2.A2.description: Entrepreneurship (CAPS G8 T3) — Forms of ownership: Companies and close corporations.
EMS.G8.B2.A2.recovery_strategy: A company is a separate legal 'person' owned by shareholders.

questions.question: What is a company?
options: A business that is a separate legal 'person', owned by shareholders
A business owned by one person only
questions.expected: A business that is a separate legal 'person', owned by shareholders
questions.memo: A company is a separate legal entity owned by shareholders.

questions.question: Who owns a company?
questions.memo: Shareholders own a company through their shares.

questions.question: What is the difference between a private and a public company?
options: A public company can sell shares to the general public; a private one cannot
A private company is bigger always
questions.expected: A public company can sell shares to the general public; a private one cannot
questions.memo: Public companies can offer shares to the public; private companies cannot.

questions.question: A close corporation (CC) was traditionally owned by ____.
questions.memo: Close corporations were owned by a small number of members.

questions.question: An advantage of a company is that ____.
options: it can raise large amounts of capital by selling shares
questions.expected: it can raise large amounts of capital by selling shares
questions.memo: Companies can raise big capital by issuing shares.
