questions.question: Households and businesses are the main participants in a closed economy's circular flow.
questions.memo: The simple flow is between households and businesses.

questions.question: Households supply factors of production like labour to businesses.
questions.memo: Households provide labour and other factors.

questions.question: A closed economy trades freely with other countries.
questions.memo: A closed economy has no foreign trade.

questions.question: Businesses provide households with goods and services.
questions.memo: Businesses produce goods and services for households.

questions.question: The two main participants in a closed economy are households and ____.
questions.memo: Households and businesses are the participants.

questions.question: Households supply ____ of production, like labour, to businesses.
questions.memo: Households supply factors of production.

questions.question: An economy with no foreign trade is a ____ economy.
questions.memo: A closed economy has no foreign trade.

questions.question: Businesses provide households with goods and ____.
questions.memo: Businesses provide goods and services.

questions.question: Sort each role under 'Households' or 'Businesses'.
questions.expected: Households supply labour and buy goods; businesses produce goods and pay wages.
questions.memo: Households supply factors and consume; businesses produce and pay for factors.

items.text: Households spend wages on goods and services
Businesses receive that money as income

EMS.G9.E2.A2.title: Flows of money, goods and factors
EMS.G9.E2.A2.description: The Economy (CAPS G9 T1) — The circular flow: Flows of money, goods and factors.
EMS.G9.E2.A2.recovery_strategy: Money flows one way, goods and factors the other — a closed loop.

questions.question: In the circular flow, money flows in ____ to goods and factors.
questions.memo: Money flows one way while goods and factors flow the other — opposite directions.

questions.question: Wages flowing from businesses to households are a flow of ____.
questions.memo: Wages are a money flow from businesses to households.

questions.question: Labour flowing from households to businesses is a flow of ____.
questions.memo: Labour is a factor of production flowing to businesses.

questions.question: Goods and services flow from ____ to ____.
questions.memo: Businesses produce goods and services that flow to households.

questions.question: Spending by households on goods is a flow of ____ to businesses.
questions.memo: Household spending is a money flow to businesses.

questions.question: The circular-flow diagram shows ____.
options: the two-way flows of money, goods and factors
questions.expected: the two-way flows of money, goods and factors
questions.memo: The diagram shows money flowing one way and goods/factors the other.

questions.question: Which is a 'real' flow (not money)?
questions.memo: Real flows are goods and factors (like labour); money flows are the opposite.

questions.question: Which is a money flow?
questions.memo: Wages and spending are money flows.

questions.question: Why must the flows balance in a closed economy?
options: What households spend becomes business income, and wages return to households
questions.expected: What households spend becomes business income, and wages return to households
questions.memo: Money circulates: spending becomes income, wages become spending — it loops.

questions.question: The flows are drawn as arrows going in ____ around the loop.
questions.memo: Money goes one way; goods and factors go the other.

questions.question: Money flows in the opposite direction to goods and factors in the circular flow.
questions.memo: Money flows one way; goods and factors flow the other.

questions.question: Wages are a money flow from businesses to households.
questions.memo: Businesses pay wages (money) to households.

questions.question: Goods and services flow from households to businesses.
questions.memo: Goods and services flow from businesses to households.

questions.question: Household spending is a money flow to businesses.
questions.memo: Spending sends money from households to businesses.

questions.question: Money flows in the ____ direction to goods and factors.
questions.memo: Money flows opposite to goods and factors.

questions.question: Wages are a flow of ____ from businesses to households.
questions.memo: Wages are a money flow.

questions.question: Labour is a ____ flowing from households to businesses.
questions.memo: Labour is a factor of production.

questions.question: Goods and services flow from businesses to ____.
questions.memo: Goods flow to households.

questions.question: Sort each flow into 'Money flow' or 'Real flow (goods/factors)'.
questions.expected: Wages and spending are money flows; labour and goods are real flows.
questions.memo: Money flows = wages and spending; real flows = labour and goods (the opposite direction).

questions.question: Put one loop of money around the circular flow in order.

items.text: Business pays wages (money) to a household
The household spends the money on goods
The money becomes the business's income
The business uses it to pay wages again

questions.memo: Wages → spending → business income → wages again — money loops continuously.

EMS.G9.E3.A1.title: The law of demand
EMS.G9.E3.A1.description: The Economy (CAPS G9 T2) — Price theory: The law of demand.
EMS.G9.E3.A1.recovery_strategy: Demand: when price goes up, quantity wanted goes down.

questions.question: What does the law of demand say?
options: When the price rises, the quantity demanded usually falls
questions.expected: When the price rises, the quantity demanded usually falls
questions.memo: Higher prices generally reduce the quantity consumers want to buy.

questions.question: If the price of a good falls, the quantity demanded usually ____.
questions.memo: Lower prices usually increase the quantity demanded.

questions.question: A demand schedule is ____.
options: a table of prices and the quantities demanded
questions.expected: a table of prices and the quantities demanded
questions.memo: A demand schedule lists quantities demanded at different prices.

questions.question: The demand curve usually slopes ____.
questions.memo: Because higher prices mean lower quantity demanded, the curve slopes down.

questions.question: At a higher price, consumers generally buy ____.
questions.memo: Higher prices reduce the quantity demanded.

questions.question: Which is an example of the law of demand?
options: A shop drops its price and sells more units
A shop raises its price and sells more
questions.expected: A shop drops its price and sells more units
questions.memo: Lower price → more units sold illustrates the law of demand.

questions.question: 'Quantity demanded' means ____.
options: how much consumers will buy at a given price
the cost to make a good
questions.expected: how much consumers will buy at a given price
questions.memo: Quantity demanded is how much consumers buy at a particular price.

questions.question: Why do consumers buy less when prices rise?
questions.memo: Higher prices make goods less affordable, lowering quantity demanded.

questions.question: On a demand graph, price is usually on the ____ axis.
questions.memo: Price is plotted on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal.

questions.question: Which statement matches the law of demand?
options: Price up → quantity demanded down; price down → quantity demanded up
questions.expected: Price up → quantity demanded down; price down → quantity demanded up
questions.memo: Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.

questions.question: According to the law of demand, higher prices usually mean lower quantity demanded.
questions.memo: Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.

questions.question: A demand schedule is a table of prices and quantities demanded.
questions.memo: It lists quantity demanded at each price.

questions.question: The demand curve usually slopes upwards.
questions.memo: The demand curve slopes downwards (higher price, lower quantity).

questions.question: Lower prices usually increase the quantity demanded.
questions.memo: Cheaper goods are bought in greater quantity.

questions.question: The law of demand says higher prices lead to ____ quantity demanded.
questions.memo: Higher price → lower quantity demanded.

questions.question: A table of prices and quantities demanded is a demand ____.
questions.memo: A demand schedule is such a table.

questions.question: The demand curve slopes ____.
questions.memo: The demand curve slopes down.

questions.question: When price falls, quantity demanded usually ____.
questions.memo: Lower price → higher quantity demanded.

questions.question: Sort each into 'Increases quantity demanded' or 'Decreases quantity demanded'.
questions.expected: Lower prices raise quantity demanded; higher prices lower it.
questions.memo: Law of demand: lower price → more demanded; higher price → less demanded.

questions.question: Put this demand example in order (a shop running a sale).

items.text: A shop lowers the price of a drink
More customers want to buy it

questions.memo: Lower price → more affordable → more buyers → quantity demanded rises.

EMS.G9.E3.A2.title: The law of supply
EMS.G9.E3.A2.description: The Economy (CAPS G9 T2) — Price theory: The law of supply.
EMS.G9.E3.A2.recovery_strategy: Supply: when price goes up, quantity offered goes up.

questions.question: What does the law of supply say?
options: When the price rises, the quantity supplied usually rises
questions.expected: When the price rises, the quantity supplied usually rises
questions.memo: Higher prices encourage producers to supply more.

questions.question: If the price of a good falls, the quantity supplied usually ____.
questions.memo: Lower prices usually reduce the quantity producers supply.

questions.question: A supply schedule is ____.
options: a table of prices and quantities supplied
questions.expected: a table of prices and quantities supplied
questions.memo: A supply schedule lists quantities supplied at different prices.

questions.question: The supply curve usually slopes ____.
questions.memo: Higher prices → more supplied, so the supply curve slopes up.

questions.question: Why do producers supply more when prices rise?
options: Higher prices mean more profit, so they produce more
questions.expected: Higher prices mean more profit, so they produce more
questions.memo: Higher prices raise potential profit, encouraging more production.

questions.question: Which is an example of the law of supply?
options: Prices rise, so a farmer plants more crops to sell
Prices rise, so a farmer plants less
questions.expected: Prices rise, so a farmer plants more crops to sell
questions.memo: Higher prices encourage producing more — the law of supply.

questions.question: 'Quantity supplied' means ____.
options: how much producers will offer at a given price
questions.expected: how much producers will offer at a given price
questions.memo: Quantity supplied is how much producers offer at a price.

questions.question: At a lower price, producers generally supply ____.
questions.memo: Lower prices reduce the quantity supplied.

questions.question: Which statement matches the law of supply?
options: Price up → quantity supplied up; price down → quantity supplied down
Price has no effect on supply
questions.expected: Price up → quantity supplied up; price down → quantity supplied down
questions.memo: Price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.

questions.question: Demand and supply curves slope in ____ directions.
questions.memo: Demand slopes down; supply slopes up — opposite directions.

questions.question: According to the law of supply, higher prices usually mean a higher quantity supplied.
questions.memo: Price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.

questions.question: A supply schedule is a table of prices and quantities supplied.
questions.memo: It lists quantity supplied at each price.

questions.question: The supply curve usually slopes downwards.
questions.memo: The supply curve slopes upwards (higher price, more supplied).

questions.question: Producers usually supply more when they can earn a higher price.
questions.memo: Higher prices encourage more production.

questions.question: The law of supply says higher prices lead to ____ quantity supplied.
questions.memo: Higher price → higher quantity supplied.

questions.question: A table of prices and quantities supplied is a supply ____.
questions.memo: A supply schedule lists quantity supplied at each price.

questions.question: The supply curve slopes ____.
questions.memo: The supply curve slopes up.

questions.question: When price rises, quantity supplied usually ____.
questions.memo: Higher price → more supplied.

questions.question: Sort each into 'Increases quantity supplied' or 'Decreases quantity supplied'.

items.text: Producers can earn more per unit

questions.expected: Higher prices raise quantity supplied; lower prices reduce it.
questions.memo: Law of supply: higher price → more supplied; lower price → less supplied.

questions.question: Put this supply example in order (rising prices).

items.text: The market price of tomatoes rises

questions.memo: Higher price → more profit → more produced → quantity supplied rises.

EMS.G9.E3.A3.title: Equilibrium and shifts
EMS.G9.E3.A3.description: The Economy (CAPS G9 T2) — Price theory: Equilibrium and shifts.
EMS.G9.E3.A3.recovery_strategy: Equilibrium is where the demand and supply curves cross.

questions.question: What is the equilibrium price?
options: The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
questions.expected: The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
questions.memo: Equilibrium is where demand and supply are equal.

questions.question: At equilibrium, the demand and supply curves ____.
questions.memo: Equilibrium is the point where the two curves cross.

questions.question: If demand increases (more people want a good), the price tends to ____.
questions.memo: More demand usually pushes the price up.

questions.question: If supply increases (more is available), the price tends to ____.
questions.memo: More supply usually pushes the price down.

questions.question: A 'change in quantity demanded' is caused by ____.
options: a change in the good's own price
questions.expected: a change in the good's own price
questions.memo: Quantity demanded changes when the good's own price changes.

questions.question: If demand falls while supply stays the same, price tends to ____.
questions.memo: Less demand with steady supply pushes price down.

questions.question: If supply falls (e.g. a drought) while demand stays the same, price tends to ____.
questions.memo: Less supply with steady demand pushes price up.

questions.question: Equilibrium is important because ____.
options: it is where the market 'clears' with no shortage or surplus
questions.expected: it is where the market 'clears' with no shortage or surplus
questions.memo: At equilibrium there is no shortage or surplus — the market clears.

questions.question: If the price is above equilibrium, there is usually a ____.
questions.memo: Above equilibrium, supply exceeds demand — a surplus.

questions.question: If the price is below equilibrium, there is usually a ____.
questions.memo: Below equilibrium, demand exceeds supply — a shortage.

questions.question: Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
questions.memo: It is the balance point of demand and supply.

questions.question: At equilibrium the demand and supply curves cross.
questions.memo: Equilibrium is the intersection of the curves.

questions.question: An increase in demand tends to lower the price.
questions.memo: An increase in demand tends to raise the price.

questions.question: An increase in supply tends to lower the price.
questions.memo: More supply pushes the price down.

questions.question: The price where demand equals supply is the ____ price.
questions.memo: Equilibrium price balances demand and supply.

questions.question: At equilibrium, the demand and supply curves ____.
questions.memo: The curves intersect at equilibrium.

questions.question: An increase in demand tends to make the price ____.
questions.memo: More demand raises price.

questions.question: An increase in supply tends to make the price ____.
questions.memo: More supply lowers price.

questions.question: Sort each change by its usual effect on the equilibrium price.
questions.expected: More demand or less supply raises price; more supply or less demand lowers it.
questions.memo: Price up: demand↑ or supply↓. Price down: supply↑ or demand↓.

questions.question: Put the path to a new higher equilibrium price in order (demand rises).

items.text: More consumers want the good (demand increases)
At the old price there is now a shortage
A new, higher equilibrium price is reached

questions.memo: Demand rises → shortage at old price → price rises → new equilibrium.

EMS.G9.E4.A1.title: What trade unions are
EMS.G9.E4.A1.description: The Economy (CAPS G9 T3) — Trade unions: What trade unions are.
EMS.G9.E4.A1.recovery_strategy: A trade union is workers joining together to bargain as one.

questions.question: What is a trade union?
options: An organisation of workers who join together to protect their interests
A type of business that sells goods
questions.expected: An organisation of workers who join together to protect their interests
questions.memo: A trade union is workers organised together to protect and advance their interests.

questions.question: Workers join a trade union mainly to ____.
options: bargain together for better wages and conditions
questions.expected: bargain together for better wages and conditions
questions.memo: Unions let workers bargain collectively for better pay and conditions.

questions.question: 'Collective bargaining' means ____.
options: workers negotiating as a group with employers
questions.expected: workers negotiating as a group with employers
questions.memo: Collective bargaining is group negotiation between workers and employers.

questions.question: Trade unions developed historically because ____.
options: individual workers had little power against employers
questions.expected: individual workers had little power against employers
questions.memo: Unions grew so workers could gain bargaining power together.

questions.question: A trade union represents ____.
questions.memo: A union represents the interests of its worker members.

questions.question: Which is something a trade union might negotiate?
questions.memo: Unions negotiate for better pay and safer working conditions.

questions.question: Why is there 'strength in numbers' for a union?
options: Many workers together have more bargaining power than one alone
One worker is stronger than many
questions.expected: Many workers together have more bargaining power than one alone
questions.memo: A united group has far more bargaining power than a single worker.

questions.question: A union member pays ____ to belong to the union.
questions.memo: Members usually pay subscriptions to fund the union.

questions.question: Which best describes a trade union?
options: A group of workers acting together for shared interests
questions.expected: A group of workers acting together for shared interests
questions.memo: A union is workers organised for their shared interests.

questions.question: Historically, unions helped workers gain ____.
options: rights like fair pay and safer workplaces
questions.expected: rights like fair pay and safer workplaces
questions.memo: Unions historically won better pay, conditions and rights.

questions.question: A trade union is an organisation of workers protecting their interests.
questions.memo: Unions organise workers to protect their interests.

questions.question: Collective bargaining means workers negotiate as a group.
questions.memo: It is group negotiation with employers.

questions.question: Trade unions represent employers, not workers.
questions.memo: Trade unions represent workers, not employers.

questions.question: Workers have more bargaining power together than alone.
questions.memo: There is strength in numbers in bargaining.

questions.question: An organisation of workers protecting their interests is a trade ____.
questions.memo: A trade union organises workers.

questions.question: Workers negotiating together as a group is called ____ bargaining.
questions.memo: Collective bargaining is group negotiation.

questions.question: A trade union represents its worker ____.
questions.memo: Unions represent their members.

questions.question: Members usually pay ____ to belong to a union.
questions.memo: Members pay subscription fees.

questions.question: Sort each statement as 'True of trade unions' or 'False of trade unions'.

items.text: They aim to lower their members' wages

questions.expected: Unions represent workers and bargain collectively; they are not employer-owned and do not aim to cut members' wages.
questions.memo: Unions = worker-led, collective bargaining, better pay/conditions.

questions.question: Put the steps of forming and using a trade union in order.

items.text: Workers realise they have little power alone
They join together to form a union
The union bargains collectively with the employer
Workers gain better pay or conditions

questions.memo: Alone they're weak → unite → bargain collectively → win better pay/conditions.

EMS.G9.E4.A2.title: The role of trade unions
EMS.G9.E4.A2.description: The Economy (CAPS G9 T3) — Trade unions: The role of trade unions.
EMS.G9.E4.A2.recovery_strategy: Unions push for workers — affecting wages, conditions and the economy.

questions.question: Which is a role of a trade union?
options: Negotiating wages and working conditions for members
Setting all of a country's tax
questions.expected: Negotiating wages and working conditions for members
questions.memo: Unions negotiate pay and conditions on behalf of members.

questions.question: A 'strike' is when workers ____.
options: stop working to push for their demands
questions.expected: stop working to push for their demands
questions.memo: A strike is a work stoppage used to press demands.

questions.question: How can trade unions affect businesses?
options: They can raise wage costs but also improve worker relations
They have no effect at all
questions.expected: They can raise wage costs but also improve worker relations
questions.memo: Unions can increase wage costs but also improve cooperation and morale.

questions.question: A responsibility of a trade union is to ____.
options: act lawfully and in members' genuine interests
questions.expected: act lawfully and in members' genuine interests
questions.memo: Unions should act lawfully and truly serve members' interests.

questions.question: How can trade unions contribute to sustainable growth?
options: By promoting fair pay and stable, productive workplaces
questions.expected: By promoting fair pay and stable, productive workplaces
questions.memo: Fair pay and stable workplaces can support productivity and growth.

questions.question: A possible downside of frequent strikes is ____.
questions.memo: Strikes can cause lost production and income for firms and workers.

questions.question: Trade unions in South Africa are part of ____.
questions.memo: Unions are part of South Africa's labour relations framework.

questions.question: Which is a benefit unions can bring workers?
questions.memo: Unions push for safer conditions and better treatment.

questions.question: How might a union and employer reach agreement without a strike?
questions.memo: Negotiation and compromise can settle disputes without strikes.

questions.question: Why must unions balance demands with the health of the business?
options: If a business fails, members lose their jobs
Members want the business to close
questions.expected: If a business fails, members lose their jobs
questions.memo: Demands that sink a business cost members their jobs, so balance matters.

questions.question: Trade unions negotiate wages and conditions for their members.
questions.memo: Negotiating pay and conditions is a core union role.

questions.question: A strike is when workers stop working to push for demands.
questions.memo: Strikes are work stoppages used to press demands.

questions.question: Trade unions can affect businesses' wage costs.
questions.memo: Union-negotiated wages can raise a business's costs.

questions.question: Frequent strikes have no effect on production.
questions.memo: Strikes can cause significant lost production and income.

questions.question: Unions negotiate ____ and working conditions for members.
questions.memo: Unions negotiate wages and conditions.

questions.question: A work stoppage to push for demands is a ____.
questions.memo: A strike is a work stoppage.

questions.question: Fair pay and stable workplaces can support sustainable ____.
questions.memo: These can support sustainable growth.

questions.question: Unions should act ____ and in members' genuine interests.
questions.memo: Unions should act lawfully and responsibly.

questions.question: Sort each effect of trade unions into 'Positive' or 'Negative' for the economy/business.

items.text: Lost production during a long strike
Higher wage costs that may reduce profit

questions.expected: Safer conditions and fairer wages are positive; lost production and higher costs are negative.
questions.memo: Unions bring benefits (safety, fair pay) and costs (strikes, higher wage costs).

questions.question: Put a wage negotiation that avoids a strike in order.

items.text: The union presents its wage demand
An agreement is reached without a strike

questions.memo: Demand → counter-offer → compromise → agreement, avoiding a strike.

EMS.G9.F1.A1.title: Cash transactions of a trading business
EMS.G9.F1.A1.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G9 T1) — Cash journals (sole trader): Cash transactions of a trading business.
EMS.G9.F1.A1.recovery_strategy: A trading business buys and sells stock — recorded in the cash journals.

EMS.G9.F1.A2.title: Effect on the accounting equation
EMS.G9.F1.A2.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G9 T1) — Cash journals (sole trader): Effect on the accounting equation.
EMS.G9.F1.A2.recovery_strategy: Even for a trader, every transaction keeps A = OE + L balanced.

questions.question: A trading business is one that ____.
options: buys and sells stock (goods) to make a profit
questions.expected: buys and sells stock (goods) to make a profit
questions.memo: A trading business buys and resells stock to make a profit.

questions.question: When a trader receives cash for a sale, what happens to assets?
questions.memo: Receiving cash increases the asset 'cash/bank'.

questions.question: When a trader pays rent in cash, what happens?
options: Cash falls and owner's equity falls (an expense)
questions.expected: Cash falls and owner's equity falls (an expense)
questions.memo: Paying an expense reduces cash and reduces owner's equity.

questions.question: The accounting equation a trader uses is ____.
questions.memo: Traders use the same equation: A = OE + L.

questions.question: Every cash transaction of a trader keeps the equation ____.
questions.memo: Each transaction keeps A = OE + L balanced.

questions.question: If a trader buys stock for cash, what happens to total assets?
options: They stay the same (stock up, cash down)
questions.expected: They stay the same (stock up, cash down)
questions.memo: Stock (asset) rises and cash (asset) falls — total assets unchanged.

questions.question: If a trader takes a cash loan, what happens?
options: Cash (asset) and the loan (liability) both rise
questions.expected: Cash (asset) and the loan (liability) both rise
questions.memo: A cash loan raises both an asset (cash) and a liability (loan).

questions.question: Making a cash profit on a sale increases the owner's ____.
questions.memo: Profit increases owner's equity.

questions.question: Why does each transaction affect at least two items?
options: So the accounting equation stays balanced
questions.expected: So the accounting equation stays balanced
questions.memo: Touching two items keeps both sides of the equation equal.

questions.question: If a trader's assets rise by R200 and liabilities are unchanged, owner's equity ____.
questions.memo: To keep A = OE + L balanced, owner's equity must rise by R200.

questions.question: A trading business buys and sells stock to make a profit.
questions.memo: Traders buy and resell goods for profit.

questions.question: Receiving cash for a sale increases the business's assets.
questions.memo: Cash received increases assets.

questions.question: Paying rent in cash increases owner's equity.
questions.memo: Paying an expense like rent reduces cash and reduces owner's equity.

questions.question: Every cash transaction keeps the accounting equation balanced.
questions.memo: Each transaction keeps A = OE + L balanced.

questions.question: A business that buys and sells stock is a ____ business.
questions.memo: Trading businesses buy and resell stock.

questions.question: Receiving cash from a sale makes cash, an ____, increase.
questions.memo: Cash is an asset that rises when received.

questions.question: The trader's equation is Assets = Owner's equity + ____.
questions.memo: A = OE + L.

questions.question: Buying stock for cash keeps total assets the ____.
questions.memo: Stock up, cash down — total assets unchanged.

questions.question: Sort each trader's cash transaction by its effect on TOTAL assets.

items.text: Cash received from a sale (at a profit)
Take a cash loan from the bank

questions.expected: A profitable sale and a loan raise assets; paying rent lowers them; buying stock for cash leaves the total unchanged.
questions.memo: Cash/loan in = assets up; expense out = assets down; asset-for-asset swap = unchanged.

questions.question: Put the reasoning for a balanced trader transaction in order.

items.text: Identify the items it affects (e.g. cash and owner's equity)
Record equal changes on both sides

questions.memo: Identify affected items, record equal changes, and the equation stays balanced.

EMS.G9.F2.A1.title: Posting to the General Ledger
EMS.G9.F2.A1.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G9 T1) — General Ledger and Trial Balance (sole trader): Posting to the General Ledger.
EMS.G9.F2.A1.caps_topic: General Ledger and Trial Balance (sole trader)
EMS.G9.F2.A1.recovery_strategy: Posting moves the journal totals into ledger accounts.

EMS.G9.F2.A2.title: Preparing the Trial Balance
EMS.G9.F2.A2.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G9 T1) — General Ledger and Trial Balance (sole trader): Preparing the Trial Balance.
EMS.G9.F2.A2.caps_topic: General Ledger and Trial Balance (sole trader)
EMS.G9.F2.A2.recovery_strategy: The Trial Balance lists every account to check debits = credits.

EMS.G9.F3.A1.title: Credit sales, debtors and the NCA
EMS.G9.F3.A1.description: Financial Literacy (CAPS G9 T2) — Credit transactions — debtors: Credit sales, debtors and the NCA.
EMS.G9.F3.A1.recovery_strategy: A debtor owes you money; the NCA protects people who buy on credit.

questions.question: What is a credit sale?
options: A sale where the customer pays later, not immediately
A sale paid in cash now
questions.expected: A sale where the customer pays later, not immediately
questions.memo: In a credit sale, the goods are taken now and paid for later.

questions.question: Who is a 'debtor'?
options: A customer who owes the business money
questions.expected: A customer who owes the business money
questions.memo: A debtor owes the business money for goods bought on credit.

questions.question: For the business, a debtor is recorded as a(n) ____.
questions.memo: A debtor is an asset — money the business will receive.

questions.question: What is the National Credit Act (NCA)?
options: A law that protects people who buy on credit
questions.expected: A law that protects people who buy on credit
questions.memo: The NCA protects consumers and regulates credit in South Africa.

questions.question: Why does the NCA matter for credit sales?
options: It helps prevent people taking on debt they cannot repay
